answer: Four objects form the chain. 'show pm-parameter-errored-seconds' confirms the counter (units seconds, type counter). 'set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> high-threshold <value>' sets the limit on one resource instance; low-threshold/high-threshold accept a number, na or not-supported, default na. 'set pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>' does the same per resource type and its show adds default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, e.g. set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. The crossing is only reported if TCA supervision is on: 'set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true' (also carries data-supervision and supported-parameters, max 100 elements). For new resources, 'set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-tca-supervision true'. direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all).

Three objects plus a status view. 'set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true' (ntp-enabled default true, ntp-auth-enabled default false, assignment-method manual/dhcp/both, default both). 'add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted true]' where key-id is 1..65534, key-type is sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, key-value is 8..40 characters and is-trusted defaults to false, e.g. add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera. Then bind it: 'add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <n>' (IPv4, IPv6 or hostname; origin dhcp or manual, default manual; auth-key-id default not-applicable; admin-state default unlock). To check: 'show ntp ntp-active-server', then 'show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>' for auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none), reach (377 means all recent probes answered), stratum, offset, jitter, delay, poll and condition (sys.peer, reject, candidate). 'show clock time-source' should read ntp.

They act on different things. 'protection-switch [-f] operation-type=<force|lockout|manual|release> switch-target=<value> protection-group=<value>' is the operating command for protection group switching, so it is the one that moves traffic to the protection path; switch-target is not needed for the release and lockout operations. Example: protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection. 'manual-switchover [-f] resource=<AID>' moves the controller: it takes the AID of the card, e.g. manual-switchover card-1-3 (G42), card-1-5 (G32) or card-1-12 (G34c), and prompts 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. Both run in Operational mode. Confirm results with 'show protection-group-<name>' (pg-state, last-switch-trigger) or 'show controller-card' (redundancy-status active/standby/not-in-service).

'set-time' is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so an active NTP source is what rejects it. Run 'show clock': time-source reads ntp or manual (default manual), and the same output gives current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, DST-active and last-time-jump (jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). 'time' prints the system time, e.g. 2020-06-29T22:29:37+00:00, based on the configured timezone. If time-source is ntp, check 'show ntp ntp-enabled' and 'show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>' for reach, offset, stratum, auth-status and condition. To set the clock by hand, first 'set ntp ntp-enabled false', then 'set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z' (ISO 8601 combined date and time, Z for UTC) or with an offset, 'set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00'. Timezone is separate: 'set clock timezone <value>', default Universal-Time-Coordinated.

Identity: 'show ne' gives ne-id, ne-name (default '1830 GX'), ne-type (G30, G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), l0-mode-op, ne-site, ne-location, clli, contact, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), equipment-discovery-ready and recover-mode. Contents: 'status' gives the System dashboard (NE name/id/type, SW labels, uptime, management IP, alarm counts per severity, equipment counts per type), and 'status equipment [<chassis-id>]' trees out chassis, cards, toms with temperature, power, oper-state and alarms. 'show equipment', 'show card-<name>', 'show slot' and 'show inventory' give the detail. Cost of the reboot: 'restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]'. With no resource it restarts the active controller card; with no type it does a warm start. cold reboots all components and is service affecting, connectivity returns within five minutes; warm reboots the processor and is non service affecting (XMM4 loses visibility for 3 minutes); shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. tom supports cold only. It confirms unless -f is given.

The card in chassis 1 slot 2 is addressed as card-1-2 (add card-<name> required-type <type> chassis-name 1 slot-name 2). Beneath card in the AID scheme sit comm-eth, inventory, port, property, sub-component, tom and usb. Beneath port sit current-fw, serdes and supported-tom-power. The chassis itself parents inventory and slot, and slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> also parents current-fw. The pluggable is tom-<card-name>-<port-name>, e.g. tom-1-4-T1; adding it auto-creates the tributary port termination point and deleting it removes that. Its FRU inventory is read with 'show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>', for example show inventory-1-3-1, which returns hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (1..8, third-party subtypes only), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

The model capability is 'show supported-card-<card-type>': node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category (controller, line-card, fan, power-supply, other, carrier-card, blank), grid-mode-support (default general-c-band), max-power-draw in W, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support (no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate, yes-with-fixed-baud-rate), default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config (default false), supported-bands (default standardC-band) and supported-features. Companion tables are supported-slot, supported-port, supported-tom and supported-chassis. The card actually fitted is 'show card-<name>': required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, max-power-draw, power-profile, last-reboot-reason, last-reboot-time, parent-card, subcard-list, AID, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state. 'show capabilities-<name>' retrieves capabilities for a named card.

The objects must be built in order. 'add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad> [version ospfv2|ospfv3] [router-id-mode manual|use-loopback]': instance-id 0..255, version default ospfv2, router-id-mode default use-loopback, and with use-loopback an IPv4 LO-MGMT address must already be configured. 'add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>' has the pre-condition that the OSPF instance exists; ospf-area-type is normal. 'add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>' requires both the instance and the area; ospf-if-name is a leafref to an existing interface. Defaults that must match the far end: enable true, hello-interval 10 s (1..32767), router-dead-interval 40 s (4..65535), retransmission-interval 5 s, transmit-delay 1 s, ospf-cost 10, priority 1, ospf-if-routing auto, ospf-auth-enable false with ospf-auth-algorithm HMAC_SHA_256. Progress is read from 'show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<area-id>/<if-name>/<router-id>': state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, plus role drother/dr/bdr/ptp. Its pre-condition is that the neighbor NEs have instance, area and interface configured and are connected by DCN interface bridges; the neighbor entry is deleted when the OSPF interface goes down.

Per controller card, 'show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>' where location-id is chassis-slot and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, e.g. show software-load-1-5/active. It returns swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status (validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed or timeout, or status-unknown), swload-information, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. The individual pieces are 'show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>' with state installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version and description, e.g. show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg, and one level down 'show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<component>/<subcomponent>'. The bundled firmware is 'show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version'; versions differ per equipment-type. 'show controller-card' tells you which card is active.

Three per-port views. 'show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port>' is what this node sends: chassis-id-subtype chassis-component with the chassis serial number as chassis-id, port-id-subtype local with the port AID as port-id, port-description (port name), system-name (NE name), system-description and supported/enabled-capabilities router or bridge. 'show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress' is what was received: last-update, age, chassis-id, port-id, system-name, system-description and ttl; only the ingress direction is supported, and the data is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or cleared. To separate sending from receiving use 'show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress': total-frames-out versus total-frames-in, plus total-ageouts, total-discarded-frames, error-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs, last-change-time and last-clear-time, all defaulting to 0. Those counters freeze while lldp-admin-status is disabled on the port. Globally, 'show lldp hold-on-timer' defaults to 900 seconds.

'show slot' (or show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>) lists every holder with AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment; an empty installed-type and a current-equipment of --- means nothing is fitted there. For what is fitted, 'show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>' gives hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code and fw-status, which is not-applicable (no upgradeable firmware), current, not-current (at least one component behind) or unavailable. The per-component firmware level is 'show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>', returning fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status (current, not-current, unavailable; default unavailable), for example current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 against an expected 0x28 shows not-current. current-fw also hangs off card, port and slot.

'show manifest' lists the downloaded manifest files, and 'show manifest-<manifest-file>' gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ) and information. The contents are 'show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name>' with state installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), plus version and description, so that is where you see whether each piece got installed. Firmware carried in the package is 'show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version', and the packaged FRU data per equipment type is 'show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>'. Related views: 'show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name>', 'show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>' for the installed state on a card, and 'show upgrade-status-<resource>' for status (idle, validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete or failed, no-communication), step, start-time, end-time and details at NE, chassis or card level.

Alarm severity per resource type comes from alarm-severity-entry: 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>' where severity is critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning, direction is na, ingress or egress, and location is na, near-end or far-end; show also returns service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). The same entries are reachable through 'set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>', e.g. set alarm-severity-profile alarm-severity-entry-trusted-certificate/CERTIFICATE-EXPIRED severity critical. PM defaults come from pm-profile-entry: 'set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision <true|false> default-tca-supervision <true|false>' decides, for newly created resources of that type, whether PM data supervision and threshold crossing supervision start enabled. Above it, 'set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled|manual' (default manual) can enable PM data supervision globally instead of leaving it to pm-profile-entry or pm-control-entry. Both alarm-severity-profile and pm-profile are system-managed and cannot be deleted.

The deciding object is ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>. Its action attribute is protect, bypass or discard, default protect. It also carries priority (uint8, giving precedence between SPD entries), ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel or transport (default tunnel), esn default true, anti-replay-window 32..1024 default 64 when action is protect, and dynamic-ts enabled/disabled default disabled. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect. Underneath it hang ipsec-sa-proposal and ipsec-traffic-selector-.../<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> (next-layer-protocol any = 0, opaque = 255, or a number 0-255; default any). Under each traffic selector hang local-subnet and remote-subnet (an IPv4/IPv6 prefix) and local-ports and remote-ports (start is all, opaque or a port number; stop defaults to 0 and 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque). The SPD entry itself sits under ikev2-peer, which sits under ikev2-local-instance.

trusted-certificate-<id> is the CA: the X509v3 CA (root and intermediate) certificate trusted by the system, and the trust-chain leaf of the other objects is a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id. local-certificate-<id> is this node's own identity: the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the various secure application identities; it uniquely exposes used-by (secure-applications, ikev2-peers using it), self-signed and subject-alternative-names. peer-certificate-<id> is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application, and it uniquely exposes white-listed (true means it was imported with no trust chain). All three are set/show only, sharing revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto), alarm-report-control and label. The fourth, certificate, is the list and delete command: 'show certificates' lists all managed local/trusted/peer certificates and 'show certificate-revocation' the revocations.

Import with 'import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]' in Operational mode; the types are local-certificate, peer-certificate and trusted-certificate, and the input is PEM. -i imports intermediate certificates found in a PEM bundle, or those referenced by the AIA extension of a single-certificate file; root certificates have to be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given the name is derived from the topmost issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, e.g. trusted-certificate-Nokia-1 and -2. passphrase applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. Example: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <PEM string> <passphrase>. Removal is 'clear [-f] certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<cert-id>' in Operational mode, e.g. clear certificate trusted id=root, which asks 'Are you sure? [y/n]'. The id must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press tab to list eligible ids. Bulk options in place of a type are purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused.

For real traffic the deciding object is ace-<name>/<sequence-id>, the access control entry: its action is drop (default), accept or reject, matched on source-ip-address, destination-ip-address, source/destination lower and upper L4 ports, ttl (1..255, default 255) and protocol (default any), with direction input (default) or output. Evaluation order within a list comes from the ACE sequence-id, ranged 1-100 for AUX and DCN-B interfaces and 1-256 for DCN-A, recommended in multiples of 5 so rules can be inserted. acl-<name> is only the container: it sets type IPv4 or IPv6 and the interface the filter is applied to (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2, DCN-2-B) and must exist before an ACE can be added. Nothing to do with traffic: access-rule and access-rule-list control management access, permitting or denying create/read/update/delete/execute on YANG paths, RPCs, notifications and external commands per user-group. 'show access-control-list' is a read-only display.

Order is by sequence-id: the id of the access-rule within its list, used for processing all rules, and lower numbered ids are processed first, so the lower sequence-id wins. The access-rule-list itself is processed in order as given by its own sequence-id. If sequence-id is not provided on either object it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, that is, the rule goes to the end of the list; the id may be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries. On the list, user-group is a leaf-list of user-group names with a maximum of 20 user-groups referenced; the default value '*' matches all existing user-groups. Other limits worth knowing: the system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists, and the attribute and attribute-value leaf-lists on a rule allow at most 10 entries of up to 64 characters each. For IP traffic filters the equivalent ordering key is the ACE sequence-id.

The trap community string is not in snmp-community; as that command's own note states, the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. snmp-community-<name> only holds community-string (1..32 characters), enabled (default true) and community-string-access, whose only value is read-only, and that is used for polling. Traps take theirs from 'add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]'. Defaults there are trap-community-string 'infinera', snmp-version v2c (or v3, in which case snmpv3-user applies), target-port 162, target-transport udp and enabled true. Fix the rejection with 'set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>' and confirm with 'show snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string'.

external-fiber-connection is the one written by something other than you: the guide states it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it can be configured manually that is not recommended. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations, and carries src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, label, fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way (default two-way) and scope general-purpose (default) or cable-id; only entries with scope cable-id are included in CableID path verification. By contrast fiber-connection-<name> is the user-provisioned link between two distinct ports or sub-ports in the same NE, with src-port, dst-port and the same fiber-connection-type. 'show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> fiber-connection-list' shows which fiber connections support a given entity.

To address the node use ipv4-address: 'add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>', for example add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0 or add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'. origin is static (default), dhcp or auto-config; addresses beginning with 0, 127, or 224 through 255 are disallowed and only valid netmasks are accepted. The other two are read-only LLDP views and configure nothing. 'show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>' retrieves the management address advertised by the remote system on that port and direction (ingress, egress). 'show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>' is the same data for the local side, with no direction key. Both expose only if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid, and each management address must have a distinct subtype and address.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Check 'show interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method' and set it back with 'set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static' (values static and dhcp, default static); ipv4-enabled must also be true (default true). The address itself is rejected if it begins with 0 (current network), 127 (loopback) or 224 through 255 (broadcast, multicast, experimental), and only valid netmasks are accepted. To see which interfaces are available, type ? after 'ipv4-address-' and the system displays the object completion options, or run 'show interface' for if-name, if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, admin-state and oper-state. Then: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'.

Everything the node is using is under route: 'show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>' shows the list of system routes from various sources, with source-protocol naming the origin (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop none (default), blackhole or unreachable. Routes hang under a RIB, listed by 'show rib-<rib-name>' with vrf and address-family ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast; the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family per routing instance. The outgoing leg is 'show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> next-hop-address', e.g. show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN. Hand-typed routes are added with 'add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [special-next-hop blackhole]': advertised default false, distance 1..255 default 1, origin manual (default) or dhcp; show adds monitoring-state (unmonitored, ok, failed). ipv6-static-route is the v6 equivalent.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the management IPsec tunnel. Both are keyed 'local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>' (and the identical remote-ports path), so they hang under an IPsec traffic selector inside an SPD entry. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop defaults to 0, and 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53 and add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all. connection-ports is the connectivity one: 'show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]' returns the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card for that degree, and creating it creates the OMS of the corresponding dwdm port. degree-number is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; index has range 1..2 but is always 1 in 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional.

'take-snapshot [-h] [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]' makes the copy, Operational mode. db-instance is temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; type is db-backup (default, a backup slot) or system-backup (chassis storage); description is up to 128 characters. Examples: take-snapshot, take-snapshot manual description='Recover point'. Refusal: the system only accepts the command if the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption is configured, either globally via 'set security-policies db-passphrase' or as a parameter here; it must be at least 40 characters, contain no dictionary words, and use the 85-character Z85 set. Re-taking an existing instance such as oneweek overwrites the existing file. List what exists with 'show database' or 'show database-<database-type>' (active, manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback, temp) for database-state, backup-time and description. Put it back with 'activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]', db-instance default temp, sanity-check-override default false; a snapshot must have been taken before it can be activated.

activate is one operational-mode verb with several sub-parameters: swimage (activates the currently installable image, implies a system restart, db-action auto|empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback default auto), database (activates the currently inactive database, restart-type cold|warm default cold, sanity-check-override default false), location-led (entity is a chassis or card, led-mode flash|solid default flash, timeout 0..120 s default 0 meaning no timeout, only one test at a time), eqpt-fw (resource plus fw-image-name), krp (installs a Key Replacement Package), otdr, otdr-fiber-check, loopback (WSS loopback on an NMC) and activate-file. Unless -f is given you must confirm. The database-snapshot case has its own command: activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override true|false], db-instance default temp, and a snapshot must already have been taken.

Per card: show capabilities-<name>, where name is the card name; it retrieves that card's capabilities (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). Photonic layer: show l0-capabilities, which shows the capability details for the node's Layer 0 functions; it takes no parameters. Add/drop: show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs] - max-degrees is the maximum number of degrees (20, uint8; 0 if not supported, and degrees exist only on OADM node types, ILA is 0 by convention because it has just two fixed directions), max-adgs is the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups (110, uint8; 0 if not supported, OADM node types only). The maximum degree count is the maximum 'working' degree-number, not necessarily a supported deployment configuration.

Controller only: show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]. redundancy-status is active|standby|not-in-service (default not-in-service); redundancy-standby-status is ready-synchronized, not-ready-synchronizing (default), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out or card-not-present; switchover count and timestamp are visible only on the active controller. Any card in the shelf: card, the card-base object common to all card types, with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, power-profile, admin-state, last-reboot-reason and last-reboot-time. What a card model supports: show supported-card-<card-type>, giving node-type-compatibility (all|ILA|OADM), category (controller, line-card, fan, power-supply, carrier-card, blank, other), card-width, max-power-draw, location-led-support and support-serdes-config (default false).

macsec-entity is MACsec on an Ethernet facility: add/set/show/delete macsec-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (e.g. ethernet-6-3-3), enabled default true, link-security-control must-secure|should-secure default must-secure, replay-protection enable|disable, replay-protection-window 0..4294967295 default 0, and read-only negotiated-cipher-suite. secure-entity is L1/optical-line encryption: add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <value> remote-secure-entity <value> (the remote optical carrier on G40, remote ODU on G30, or remote OTUFlex), enabled default false, re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s default 28800, re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic|continue-traffic default continue-traffic, traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s default 0. Cipher terms: MACsec ones in mka-policy (macsec-cipher-suite, confidentiality-offset); optical ones in the show-only secure-entity-sa-proposal (encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521).

ase-idler-service is the per-card ASE idler filling function on the WSS: add/delete/set/show ase-idler-service-<name>, key attribute ase-idler-enable enabled|disabled (default disabled) which fills the unused and nmc-failed portions of the band, plus read-only ase-idler-state (ase-enabled, ase-partially-enabled, ase-faulted, ase-disabled, default ase-disabled) and function idler. ase-idler-source is the pump that generates the signal: set/show only, pump-enable enabled|disabled default disabled, target-output-power -3.00..20.50 dBm default 13, read-only pump-state, admin-state lock|unlock|maintenance default unlock, function ase-idler-source. sw-service does not belong with them: show sw-service-<sv-name> / show sw-services lists software services and containers on the node, with state off|ok|fail, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time and reboot-count.

No. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]enabled|disabled toggles Zero Touch Provisioning; change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, while disabled stops ZTP even if it is already running. Operational mode, prompts unless -f; check with show ztp. clear [-f] recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring traffic settings, so it may be traffic impacting; no parameters, prompts unless -f. The carrier-mode commands are read-only by contrast: show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> lists supported modes (capacity, client-mode ethernet|ethernet-otn, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id, status), and show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode> adds actual-carrier-mode, sop-tracking-mode and candidate-subtypes.

State: show third-party-app-<app-name> (also show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name>) gives state running|stopped|failed (default stopped) and enable true|false (default false; if enabled the app is started and restarts with the system, if disabled it is stopped), plus version, vendor, product, label and information (0..1024 chars). Firmware side: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> gives file-status valid|invalid|missing, path, version, crc, vendor, part-number, nsa-upgrade-version (versions from which upgrade is non-service-affecting), present-in-eqpt and applicable-eqpt (max 80 elements each). Clearing: clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>, which prompts unless -f is given. To restart rather than clear, use appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]restart|netls|exec [target=]<value> (default system) with optional parameters (max 50).

Per session: cli-session-config-<session-id>. set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value> gives more rows for that login only; cli-lines is 10..1000, default 40, the rows shown before pausing (SPACEBAR resumes). Also cli-columns 80..4000 default 80, interactive-mode true|false default true (per session, not persistent) and display-timestamp default false. The protocol as a whole is cli: enabled default true (you cannot disable CLI from within a CLI session), port 1..65535 default 22, script-dir read-only, default-interactive-mode default true (new sessions only), show-alarm-columns default default-columns with global effect. The two system-configuration objects are config (show config [entity-id|entity-type], displaying non-default configuration recursively from the current scope) and configure (enters Candidate Configuration mode, target exclusive or shared, default exclusive, optionally from-default, from-script or from-commit).

The generic assignment is set: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [...] [<filter> ...]. It changes attributes of existing managed entities, needs at least one attribute-value pair from the same entity, supports wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*) and ranges or lists (card-1-[1..4], interface-[DCN,CRAFT]), and asks for confirmation when the request may be traffic impacting or implicitly affects multiple instances; -v validates, -f forces. The set- prefixed ones are separate operations: set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>...) changes the operator state of alarms (none, ack, close; state is mandatory; 1 to 10 alarm ids; acknowledge-text 0..256 chars), and set-time [new-time=]<value> changes the system time, only applicable when the time-source is manual (NTP not enabled), in ISO 8601 form such as 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z or with +/-hh:mm. The one ending in -set is named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>, a data object whose value is a string 1..1024.

mc is the Media Channel, a user-creatable spectrum slot on an OMS: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value> in MHz, with center-frequency and slot-width calculated by the system and auto-delete disabled by default. nmc is the Network Media Channel, the carrier inside it: add nmc-<name> parent-facility <value> center-frequency <value>, center-frequency 190650000..196700000 MHz, width 15000..200000 MHz default 35000 (set to the 3 dB signal bandwidth matching the transponder baud rate). For both, the supporting card must be part of a Degree, not an ADG. The fillers are show-only objects the system creates for unused spectrum: mc-f reports lower-frequency, upper-frequency and slot-width; nmc-f reports alloc- and actual- lower/upper frequency and bandwidth (alloc-bandwidth default 75000 MHz), power-actual-tx/rx and monitoring-state, and allows only admin-state and alarm-report-control to be set.

What runs the scan: activate otdr [entity=]<port> [[otdr-file-prefix=]<value>], or activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> for a manual OTDR-based fiber check (used when automatic OTDR is disabled; runs up to 3 tests and errors if a scan is already in progress). Where you tune it: otdr-ptp - otdr-range auto or 0..300.0 km, otdr-pulse-width auto or 10..20000 ns, otdr-measurement-speed fast|medium|slow|precision|auto|high-precision (default auto), otdr-ior auto or 1.0..2.0, otdr-fiber-type (auto, SSMF, SMF-ULL, LEAF...), otdr-resolution auto or 0.4..100.0, otdr-direction-mode default counter-prop-in-service, peak-power auto or 5..14.5, launching-fiber-length 0..50 m default 0. Where the answer comes out: otdr-ptp otdr-fiber-break-distance (break distance in km, not-available if none found), otdr-last-measurement and otdr-last-measurement-file (the .sor file). Live status is on otdr: otdr-state not-available|idle|measuring|finished|fail, otdr-measurement-port, otdr-measurement-direction, otdr-error.

The entry that keeps coming back is DHCP-assigned. Each dns-server-<address> has origin: dhcp means the address was assigned by a DHCP server, manual means it was configured by hand; default manual. Convert it with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. What the node accepts at all is dns assignment-method, which is manual, dhcp or both, default both; set it to manual to stop DHCP-learned servers being installed. dns also has enabled (default true) and search (must contain at least one dot, 0..64 chars, cleared with an empty string). For the relay two things must line up: global dhcp-relay has mode disabled|ipv4|ipv6, default disabled, plus server-address (at least one address must be configured when enabled); and per interface if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true|false, default false, which obeys the global dhcp-relay settings. A relay that does nothing usually means mode is still disabled or the interface flag is still false.

clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>] wipes the system and resets it to factory configuration, doing a secure wipe of the system data. The three types are: factory-reset, which resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations, and may imply loss of connectivity; full-wipe, which cleans the entire system and reinstalls the software on the controller and line cards, removing all files, configurations and software, requiring a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover; and inactive, which only clears the inactive software partition and so leaves the running system, its data and its configuration in place. target may be the whole system (the default) or a chassis/card AID; restart-behavior is restart (default) or shutdown. factory-reset with shutdown is not supported on L0 cards, and factory-reset does not take effect on G30 OCC2T/OCC2E. For a simple database wipe use clear database.

Read show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>, which lists inventory detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis configuration. It reports hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (1..16 chars), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and detection-timestamp, the last being when the Node Controller last detected the unprovisioned equipment; if the equipment is the chassis itself the slot-name is empty. Pair it with show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port>, which shows the dynamically discovered links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE and gives src-chassis, dst-chassis and src-chassis-state/dst-chassis-state, each node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned. Ports on a commissioned chassis appear as the port AID, ports on an unprovisioned chassis as <chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>.

The attribute is amplifier control-mode: auto-max-pw (the auto mode targeting maximum output power, and the default) or manual, where you set the gain with gain-target (0..40 dB, default 0.0, for constant-gain mode). amp-control-support reports whether auto is offered at all (auto, or manual-only). In auto mode bias the result with gain-adjustment (-20.00..20.00 dB, default 0, only on amplifiers with function pa or inline). gain-range-control follows control-mode: manual forces it to manual, auto-max-pw forces it to auto. What stops output entirely: amplifier-enable disabled (the default) - output also depends on the OSC signal for ILA node type and on OMS facilities plus an existing OXcon for OADM; forced-shutdown true (dual-band cards); admin-state lock; and an input OLOS, which after olos-shutdown-soak-timer (0..2000 ms, default 0) triggers shutdown unless olos-shutdown-disable is true. amplifier-mode is always constant-gain.

Which member is live: show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> state, which is active, standby, available or unknown, together with role (working or protection) and transport-entity. At group level show protection-group-<name> pg-state gives no-request, forced-to-working/protection, manual-to-working/protection, sf-on-working/protection, sd-on-working/protection, wait-to-restore, protection-lockout, frozen, do-not-revert or unavailable (default), plus last-switch-trigger and remaining-wtr. The switch behaviour settings are all on protection-group: protection-type y-cable|snc-n default y-cable, switching-mode unidirectional|bidirectional default unidirectional, reversion-mode revertive|non-revertive default non-revertive, hold-off-timer 0..10000 ms default 0, wtr-timer 60..720 s default 300 (revertive only), and the triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger and network-side-sd-trigger, all disabled by default. Operate a switch with protection-switch [-f] operation-type=force|lockout|manual|release.

Trigger with verify [-f] [type-select=]fiber-connection [[target-select=]<port-id>] [allow-switching]. With no port-id all paths are verified; allow-switching defaults to false - true lets CableID initiate OPSM switching so both active and inactive paths are checked, false checks active paths only. Pre-condition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be enabled. It prompts unless -f, is non-blocking, and raises CID-verification-in-progress against the NE until all queued requests finish. Watch progress with show cable-id-status: cable-id-state idle|running-incl-switching|running-no-switching, and test-progress as 'N out of M completed'. Per-pair results are in show cable-id-path-<name>: last-test-status not-verified|pass|fail in each direction, path-status enabled|disabled, last-test-qualifier up-to-date|out-dated, last-test-timestamp, and additional-info (Cable-ID TxLOS, RxLOS, Cable-ID-MISMATCH for a misconnected fibre, RxLOF, power out-of-range, timeout). show -r adds the supporting fiber connections; abort with terminate cable-id.

Where authentication is sent is decided by aaa-server: add/set aaa-server-<server-name> protocol-supported RADIUS|TACACSPLUS (default RADIUS), server-address, server-priority 1..10, enabled true|false (default true), role-supported (authentication, authorization, accounting by default), shared-secret (max 64 characters, longer is rejected, shown as *), source-ip for RADIUS communications, and ports server-port default 49, server-port-authentication default 1812, server-port-accounting default 1813. Whether remote AAA is consulted at all is security-policies aaa-authentication-method: local-only (default), local-first-then-remote, remote-first-then-local, or remote-unavailable-then-local. What happens when the server does not answer is governed by aaa-server timeout (1..90 s, default 5) and retry (0..5), with total wait timeout x (retry + 1) required to be under 5 minutes. show aaa-statistics-<server-name> counts connection-failures, which include unavailable servers and timeouts.

For key-based login by the automation account use ssh-authorized-key: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]. Each entry holds a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication; user-name 0..32 chars (local or remote user), key-id 1..64, public-key OpenSSH/PEM up to 2048 chars, public-key-algorithm read-only (ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521, ssh-rsa2048/3072/4096). Also set security-policies ssh-authentication-method to public-key or public-key-or-password (default password). For the remote host the node copies files to, use ssh-known-host: add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value>, algorithms as above plus ssh-ed25519 (from R9.0); enforcement is security-policies ssh-strict-host-key-checking, strict or relaxed, default relaxed. The node's own identity is ssh-host-key (show-only, one per algorithm), generated by ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<label>] [-t=rsa|ecdsa|ed25519], default rsa.

The key agreement policy lives in mka-policy: add/set mka-policy-<name> with key-server-priority (used by MKA to select the key server), macsec-cipher-suite (cipher suites for Secure Association Key derivation) and confidentiality-offset (octets of the Ethernet frame sent unencrypted). It is referenced from the entity via macsec-mka: set macsec-mka-<name> mka-policy <value>, which also carries connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (0..64 chars), psk-lifetime/psk-expiration-warning 1..173 days default 14, psk-lifetime-enable, and read-only is-key-server (default false). Session key rollover is mka-policy sak-rekey-interval, in seconds, range 0 or 30..65535, default 30 s. Watch the channels with show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index>: sci-tx/sci-rx (16-char hex SCI), state in-use or not-in-use as returned by the MKA stack, association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number. macsec-entity also reports negotiated-cipher-suite.

NETCONF: set/show netconf - enabled default true (you cannot disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session), port default 830 (range 1..65535, over ssh), hello-timeout 1..3600 s default 2 (the session is dropped if no hello PDU is exchanged in that time), annotate-cli-name default false. gNMI/gRPC: set/show grpc - enabled default true, port default 50051, gnmi-get-encoding-granularity per-path or per-object, default per-object. Neither is off out of the box. RESTCONF is the one with a piece disabled by default: enabled default true and https-enabled default true on https-port 8181, but http-enabled defaults to false (HTTP access is not supported in secure mode) on http-port 8080, with cookie-timeout 1..300 minutes default 5 and read-only api-root. For reference the CLI itself listens on port 22. grpc is system managed and cannot be manually deleted.

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] restarts a specific resource and prompts for confirmation unless -f is given. Omit resource-id and the active node controller card is restarted; omit type and a warm restart is done by default. So 'restart card-1-4' is warm: it reboots the card processor and is non service affecting, with connectivity regained within five minutes. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting (connectivity back within five minutes); shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. You cannot assume every card behaves the same - the guide states not all cards support all restart types, and gives counter-examples: a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, while cold reboot of CHM6/UCM4 is service affecting; warm reboot of XMM4 is non-service affecting but loses visibility for 3 minutes. Restartable entities: card (cold, warm, shutdown), card sub-component (cold, warm), tom (cold only). List sub-components with show card resources.

Three things. First the global switch: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates enabled (enabled/disabled, default disabled). Template application depends on this flag being true; enabling it does not retro-apply templates, they apply from that moment onward, and disabling it keeps the existing serdes configuration on all TOMs. Second a template keyed on part number: add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>], tom-part-number 1..16 chars, ports-applicable 'all' (the default consideration) or up to 20 port names such as T1, T10. Third the values: add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<entry-name> value <value>, one per serdes parameter (RxAmplitude, RxEQ, TxEQ, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQAdaptive). When a TOM with that part-number is plugged in the template is applied automatically; manual serdes settings are kept even if they deviate, and swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets serdes and re-applies the new template. Force re-application with apply-template. Card support is shown by supported-card support-serdes-config (default false).

OTS, the Optical Transport Section, is the fibre span between nodes: fiber-type-tx/rx, fiber-length-tx/rx, span-loss-reference, span-loss-transmit/receive, external-attenuation-tx/rx, raman coefficients, target-power-setting, osc-compatibility osc-g30 (default) or osc-7100, osc-less, laser-safety-mode. OMS, the Optical Multiplex Section, is the multiplexed DWDM band on it: monitoring-mode (intrusive by default, not-monitored for ILA, integrated-equalization for hyperscale ILA), grid-mode (flexible by default, or fixed-50G-96ch, fixed-75G-64ch, fixed-100G-48ch, fixed-150G-40ch), lower-frequency 191300000 and upper-frequency 196150000 MHz, attenuation-control-mode-rx/tx default auto. OPS, the Optical Physical Section, is the individual physical port: role tributary, multi-carrier, general-purpose (default), ase-input or active-multi-carrier; input-psd-profile -30..-6 default -6. OSC carries the supervisory traffic: osc-mode OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE for HSC OLS, osc-control auto (default) or manual, target-output-power -2.5..4.5 dBm, voa-attenuation-target-rx 0..30 dB default 10, l0-comm-interface-type ipv4 or ipv6, lof-soak-timer short|long.

The behaviour is configured on trib-ptp, in tributary-disable-action: it defines what the node does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed. The default is laser-shut-off, so the node turns the client laser off. The alternatives insert a replacement signal instead: none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais, and send-nos (1830 GX G30 only). Command: set trib-ptp-<name> tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off. Delay it with tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, 0..10000 ms, default 0 meaning hold-off disabled; it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff, holding the optical signal until the timer expires. Related switches on the same object: near-end-tda enabled|disabled default disabled, tda-degrade-mode enabled|disabled default disabled, and forward-defect-trigger true|false default true, which decides whether a received client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS flows through to the line side or triggers an egress TDA action.

Every facility carries managed-by (system or user, default system); only user-created facilities can be user deleted. trib-ptp, line-ptp, ethernet, otu, odu and flexo-group all report it. The high order ODU is created automatically by the system when an SCH (super-channel) is created, so on a CHM6 with an OTU configured use `show odu` to confirm it exists. The `add odu` page states the pre-condition explicitly: Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added. You then add the low order ODUs by hand, for example `add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu 1-7-L1-1-ODUCni time-slots 1..80`, and the digital service with `add xcon-<name> source <client> destination <line ODU>`; xcon defaults to managed-by user.

`bert` runs the Bit Error Rate Test, in Operational mode: `bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10`, then `bert stop test-id=TestX` (test-id is mandatory on stop), `bert get`, `bert delete`. test-duration minimum is 10 seconds, maximum 1000 hours, and 0 means indefinite. Test patterns are injected on the facility itself: test-signal-type on ethernet and odu-diagnostics takes none (default), PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31 or PRBS31NONINV, with test-signal-direction ingress/egress/both and test-signal-monitoring true/false (default false). Loopbacks are the loopback attribute on otu, odu and ethernet: none (default), facility or terminal, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

At each end the supporting facility must already exist and a secure-entity must be bound to it: `add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <facility> remote-secure-entity <far-end AID> enabled true`. supporting-facility is the optical-carrier on 1830 GX G40, the ODU on G30, or the ODU/OTUflex for CHM7/CHM7X L1 service encryption; remote-secure-entity is the AID of the remote optical carrier, ODU or OTUflex. enabled defaults to false and alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited, so both need attention. IKE re-keying parameters: re-key-frequency 3600..86400 seconds (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy continue-traffic (default) or kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds (default 0). The X.509v3 identities must be imported first with import-certificate: the local-certificate for this node and the far end trusted remote peer certificate as a peer-certificate, plus its trusted-certificate chain.

The `telemetry` command configures the two kinds, persistent and dynamic telemetry; the object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted (`show telemetry`, `set telemetry id <string>`, id up to 4096 characters). `show subscriptions` lists the subscriptions. `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` shows each configured subscription with related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream default, once, poll), updates-only (default false) and user-access. What each one is watching is `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<path-name>`: subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode (target-defined default, on-change, sample), sample-interval and heartbeat-interval in milliseconds (default 0) and suppress-redundant (default true).

`show db-protection-scheme` reports what protects the database at rest: encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which is changed via the db-migrate RPC. Before you can take a copy, the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption must be configured, either globally with `set security-policies db-passphrase` or inline as `take-snapshot db-passphrase=***`. It requires a minimum of 40 characters (40..200), must contain no dictionary words, and allows special characters from the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Then `take-snapshot [db-instance=temp|manual|onehour|oneday|oneweek] [description=]`, list with `show database`, export with `upload database`.

`show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>` tells you whether the prefix reached the route table and where it came from: source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop, which is none for normal routes, or blackhole or unreachable, in which case no next-hop is created under the route. `show rib-<rib-name>` gives the RIB vrf and address-family (ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast); each routing instance gets one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. `show vrf-<name>` identifies the instance, with type mgmt or internal and chassis-name. `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>` gives the resolved next-hop-address, for example `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. On the static route itself, `show ipv4-static-route-<prefix>/<vrf>` reports interface (its VRF must match the route vrf), distance 1..255 (default 1), advertised (default false) and monitoring-state unmonitored/ok/failed.

Password acceptance comes from `security-policies`: strict-password-check (default true) enforces minimum length 8, at least one lower case letter, one upper case letter, one number and one symbol, and the user name cannot be part of the password; when disabled only a 1 character minimum applies. minimum-password-length is 1..200, default 8. enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of the previous 5 passwords, with password-history-size 1..200, default 5. These policies apply only to newly defined passwords. Lockout is per user: max-invalid-login consecutive invalid logins (0..255, default 5) suspends the account for suspension-time (0..1440 minutes, default 5); `show user-<name>` reports user-status lockout and failed-logins, and security-policies has disable-user-lockout. For the stuck session, run `show session`, then `kill-session <ip-address>:<port>`; it cannot be your own session.

`show syslog` defaults: remote-logging-switch true, source-address localhost, log-file-message-coalescence true, log-relay false, assignment-method both, niap-compliant-logging false, privacy-mode false, alarm-report-control allowed. Local files via `log-file` default to source-facilities all with severity informational and above; number-of-files retained defaults to 10 (range 1..20) and max-file-size to 30 MB (range 1..30), and when a file hits max size the oldest files are discarded once the total exceeds number-of-files. The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. Console logging is off by default: log-console enabled false. Remote collectors via `log-server` default to port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, enabled true, source-facilities all. The single switch that turns off everything remote is `set syslog remote-logging-switch false`, which disables all remote logging destinations.

`show alarm` / `show alarms` lists what is raised now, per alarm with resource, AID, alarm-type, direction, location, perceived-severity, reported-time, service-affecting, alarm-category, corrective-action and operator-state; `show current-alarms` gives number-of-alarms and last-changed. Most alarms have automatic raise and clear criteria. The small subset that must be cleared by hand is listed with `show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true` and cleared with `clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [resource=...]`, for example `clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL`; this applies only to system wide alarms not associated with a particular resource. What decides whether inhibiting reporting drops alarms already up is `set alarm-control arc-behavior`: leave-alarms (default) leaves current alarms raised when ARC is set to inhibit, clear-alarms clears them.

The Equipment dashboard shows temperature: `status equipment` lists chassis, cards per chassis with subtype and TOMs per card, with per-equipment temperature sensors and power values plus presence, oper-state and alarms (for example chassis-1 temp 25C, power 2.1/4400 W, card-1-1 temp 25C). To narrow it, give the chassis id as the filter, `status equipment 5`; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so it is either all chassis or exactly one. The underlying sensors come from PM: `show pm` gives real-time temperature (C) for cards, FAN-CTRL and PEM, chassis inlet-temperature, and fan-speed in percent. The physical reflection is the LEDs: `show leds` and `show led status` return led-<location>/<name> with status off, green, yellow, amber, red, their flashing variants, cycling, cycling-with-off or not-available.

`show ots-<name>` describes the line. span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx are the measured span losses based on OSC powers, 0..99 dB where 99 dB means OLOS, versus the configured span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive (0..80 dB, default 0; 99 dB also treated as not configured on receive). span-loss-reference selects which is used, measured (default) or configured. span-loss-alarm-threshold (0..80 dB or 99, default 99) is set autonomously by the system, is persistent across reboot, and can be refreshed with the update command in measured mode. span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0.00..10.00 dB, default 1.0, and feeds the NMC input power range and the span loss high alarm; fiber-length-derived-rx/tx and external-attenuation-rx/tx (0..30 dB) also apply. What the amplifier compensates with is `show amplifier-<name>`: gain-operating and gain-target (0..40 dB), gain-range-actual, control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, gain-adjustment -20..20 dB, span-loss-control (default enabled, and must be enabled when span-loss-reference is measured), tilt-actual, input-power-mon, output-power-mon and control-state.

Going down from the client: trib-ptp is the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver equipment and the immediate protocol layer, and above it sits the client facility (ethernet, fc, stm or a client otu). That is mapped into a low order ODU (`add odu-<name> odu-type ODU4/ODU4i/ODUflexi parent-odu <HO-ODU>`), and the low order ODU is joined to the line by an xcon, whose network-mapping names the server layer (ODUCn, ODUCni, ODU4i, ODUflexi). The high order ODU sits under the line otu / flexo-group, which sits on the line-ptp. The digital to optical handover is at the line-ptp and its optical-carrier: line-system-mode openwave is described as the L1 to L0 local power control that adjusts Tx power from the L1 transponder towards the L0 line-system card (WSS, Mux or Amplifier). Below that, optical-carrier (frequency in MHz, tx-power) grouped into a super-channel is what the L0 domain carries as an nmc on a parent mc or oms, cross connected by an oxcon.

No, they are two different objects. A counter crossing a limit is PM: `add`/`set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]` sets the limit on one instance, and `set pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` sets it per resource type, exposing default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value. Whether the crossing is reported at all is tca-supervision on pm-control-entry, or default-tca-supervision on pm-profile-entry. How loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: `set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>` with critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning, or `set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>` with the same set.

Set the card object: `set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited`; the values are allowed and inhibited. The same alarm-report-control attribute exists on the facilities the card carries (trib-ptp, line-ptp, ethernet, otu, odu, flexo-group, optical-carrier, ots, amplifier), where the default is allowed, so inhibit those too if you want them silent. You can also move the card to `set card-<name> admin-state maintenance`; admin-state takes lock, unlock (default) or maintenance. What happens to the alarms it already raised is decided system wide by `set alarm-control arc-behavior`: leave-alarms, the default, leaves current alarms in a raised mode when ARC is set to inhibit; clear-alarms clears the current alarms.

`show secure-application-<id>` gives type (server or client), status enabled/disabled, active-certificate-id and in-use; in-use is a leafref to active-certificate-id and is the certificate the application presents. Assign it with `set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <cert>`, and multiple are allowed, for example `set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY`. The certificate is a local-certificate, the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing that application identity; import it with `import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=<name> <PEM string> <passphrase>`. Its CA chain must be imported as trusted-certificate first (root certificates must be installed individually; the -i flag imports intermediates from a PEM bundle), otherwise local-certificate status shows untrusted. For TLS mutual authentication set verify-client-cert to required (default disabled). For L1 encryption the far end certificate is imported as a peer-certificate.

Pipe the show command through the display filter: `show pm <command flag> | display csv` outputs CSV data importable into a spreadsheet such as Excel; display xml and display json are also available. Scope it to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter arguments (data-type, parameter, resource, resource-type, AID) and the pm-15min period; bins are selected with -sbin=<number> and -ebin=<number> (default bin 0 is current data and all bins are shown), or by time with -st= and -et= using the format 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00. -t forces a single generic table, -n= caps records per chassis (default 1000) and -s= skips records. To get files off the node instead, `upload pm-logs <file-server> <path> period=pm-15min` uploads PM data logs; without period all periods are included.

`show pm-catalog <string>` shows the contents of the PM catalog for that catalog name, for example `show pm-catalog parameter-undersized`, which returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. The same lookup per parameter is `show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]`, for example `show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds`; `show pm-parameter` on its own lists all PM parameters. Both commands are read only and are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use pm-control: `set pm-control <entity> data-supervision false`. data-supervision is real-time data supervision for that resource and takes true or false, defaulting to true. The documented example is exactly a card: `set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false`. `show pm-control` lists the configuration for all currently existing resources in the system that support PM data. The equivalent per instance attribute is `set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false`, also true/false with default true. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, pm-control-entry is keyed exactly on that scope: `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [data-supervision <value>] [tca-supervision <value>]`, so `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true` turns threshold crossing supervision on for just the 15-minute ingress near-end counters of that one resource. direction takes ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location takes all, na, near-end or far-end (default all); data-supervision and tca-supervision are true or false. `show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> supported-parameters` lists the PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, with a maximum of 100 elements.

`show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]` gives both. type is either counter or gauge. units is one of na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors or MHz. For example `show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized` returns units packets and type counter. `show pm-parameter` with no parameter lists all PM parameters, and `show pm-catalog <name>` returns the same units and type pair from the catalog. The pm-filter description also notes that a PM parameter can be either a counter or a gauge.

Yes: `set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled`. The pm-profile object holds all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. global-data-supervision takes auto-enabled, which globally enables PM data-supervision without having to toggle it individually, or manual, the default, in which the data-supervision flag is controlled via pm-profile-entry or directly per pm-control-entry. Read it back with `show pm-profile`. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

That is pm-profile-entry, which is the PM configuration per resource type: `set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true`. default-data-supervision decides, for newly created resources of that type, whether PM data supervision is automatically enabled; the companion default-tca-supervision does the same for threshold crossing supervision. Both take true or false. direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all, and location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all; period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h. Read them back with the matching `show pm-profile-entry-...`.

`show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset`, for example `show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9`. real-time-data-last-reset is a date-and-time giving the last real time data reset for that resource; if the data was never reset, it is the date and time of that resource creation. The same show also returns resource-type, AID (string, 1..64 characters), real-time-supervision (true/false, default true) and the pm-control-entry children per period, direction and location. The counters themselves are cleared with `clear pm real-time`, optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, AID, period or direction.

Use pm-threshold, which is per instance: `add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/errored-seconds high-threshold <value>`, with set to change it, show to read it and delete to remove it. period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h; direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all; location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all; parameter is the PM parameter identifier, which can be a counter or a gauge. low-threshold and high-threshold accept a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na (not applicable), or not-supported, and both default to na. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

`show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` returns default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold, the system defined default values for that parameter, plus min-value and max-value, the minimum and maximum allowed for the parameter, alongside the currently configured low-threshold and high-threshold. All of these are a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na (not applicable), or not-supported. You write the configured values with set, for example `set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200`. This object is the PM configuration per parameter for a resource type, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the clock command. Set the zone with 'set clock timezone <value>', for example 'set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]'; the value comes from the fixed list of named zones (International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00]), and the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated. To see where time comes from, use 'show clock time-source': ntp means the NE synchronises via NTP, manual means it uses its own internal clock. Default is manual. The same show also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (default false) and last-time-jump (format '<time1> to <time2>'; jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). If DNS is not properly configured, show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Use 'set ne node-type OADM'. node-type takes ILA, OADM or XPDR, and it can only be set or changed on a 1830 GX G34c chassis, which defaults to ILA; G31/G32 default to OADM and G42 to XPDR. G34c support for OADM starts at R7.0 (in R6.x it was ILA only). Preconditions for setting OADM: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be 'ila-with-equalization' or 'not-monitored', that is no spectrum (or ochm) objects may exist, and no direction-* may exist. Going the other way, to set ILA: no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be 'intrusive' (no RD or PAx card present), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note also that G34c SLTE mode (l0-mode-op slte) is supported only when node-type is ILA.

'show ne-function'. It takes no parameters and runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the NE generic functions in one output, that is the directions and the amplifiers of the node. A G30 example returns direction-1 through direction-8, then amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and finally ne-function itself.

Use the ntp command: 'set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true'. ntp-enabled is true by default; ntp-auth-enabled is false by default, so authentication must be turned on explicitly. The third settable attribute is assignment-method, which selects which configured values the system uses: manual, dhcp or both, defaulting to both. 'show ntp' returns ntp-enabled, ntp-auth-enabled, ntp-active-server (the currently active NTP server) and assignment-method. The ntp object is system managed and cannot be manually added or deleted. To complete authentication you also need a key (add ntp-key-<key-id> with is-trusted true) and the server association (set ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>). Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

NTP keys are managed with 'add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]', plus set, show and delete on the same AID. key-type, the hash algorithm used for NTP message digest computation, accepts sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, with no default. key-id is a number in the range 1..65534. key-value is a string of length 8..40. is-trusted marks the key as a trusted NTP key and takes true or false, defaulting to false. Example: 'add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera'. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. The origin attribute records the NTP address assignment method and a DHCP-configured NTP entry can be converted into a manually configured one simply by changing it: 'set ntp-server-<ip-address> origin manual'. origin takes dhcp (address assigned to the system by a DHCP server) or manual (address manually configured); the default is manual. The ip-address key may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a DNS domain name. The other settable attributes on the entry are auth-key-id (a uint32 key id, or not-applicable, which is the default), label (0..256 characters), admin-state (lock, unlock or maintenance, default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed). show also returns oper-state (default disabled) and avail-state.

Use 'show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>', for example 'show ntp-server-status-172.19.13.218'. The key field is reach: an 8-bit shift register holding the outcome of recent probes, with the most recent probe in the 2^0 position; the value 377 means all the recent probes have been answered. Supporting fields are when (seconds since the last packet was received), poll (polling interval in seconds), delay (path delay in ms), offset (clock offset to the peer in ms), jitter (path jitter in ms), stratum of the remote peer, refid (reference clock type or address), type (local, unicast, multicast or broadcast), auth-status (ok, yes, bad or none, default none) and condition (for example sys.peer, reject, candidate).

Syntax is 'restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]'. If <type> is omitted a warm start is done by default. warm reboots the processor of the CHM6, UCM4, etc. and is non service affecting; the system regains connectivity within five minutes, and a warm reboot of an XMM4 is non-service affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, also regaining connectivity within five minutes; a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost. A third type, shutdown, gracefully shuts the card down. Restartable entities: card (cold, warm, shutdown), card sub-component (cold, warm) and tom (cold); not all cards support all restart types. Omitting <resource-id> restarts the active controller card. The command asks for confirmation unless -f is given.

Because set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled. Check with 'show clock time-source' (values ntp or manual, default manual); if it reads ntp, disable synchronisation with 'set ntp ntp-enabled false' before setting the clock by hand. The new time uses a format derived from ISO 8601 with combined date and time, where Z is the UTC timezone, for example 'set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z'; a non-UTC timezone is allowed by supplying +/-hh:mm instead of Z, for example 'set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00'. Retrieve the current system time with the 'time' command, which reports it in the system configured timezone rather than the timezone used in the set-time command. set-time runs in Operational Mode.

Yes, 'status equipment'. The Equipment dashboard summarises all equipment in the system with relevant details like temperature and power usage: the list of chassis, the cards per chassis and their subtype, the toms per card, and per-equipment data including temperature sensors, power values and generic status (presence or absence, oper state, alarms). The default scope is the entire network element. On a large NE you can filter to a single chassis by passing the chassis id, for example 'status equipment 5'; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so it is either all chassis or exactly one. Output uses symbols: a check for oper-state enabled, admin-state unlocked or no alarms, a cross for oper-state disabled, and a padlock for admin-state lock. Access: Operational mode.

Use 'clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>]'. The clear system command wipes the system or a specific instance back to factory configuration and performs a secure wipe of the system data. type takes factory-reset (resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing files and user configurations, which may imply loss of connectivity), full-wipe (cleans the entire system and reinstalls SW on controller and line-cards; a base software reinstall from ONIE is required to recover) or inactive (clears the inactive software partition). target may be the entire system or a chassis/card AID; if omitted the entire system is cleared. restart-behavior is a standard restart (default) or shutdown. Limits: factory-reset does not take effect for G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported for the G30 controller card (FRCU), and clear system factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. Example: 'clear system factory-reset shutdown'. For a simple database wipe use 'clear database' instead.

Type 'time'. It takes no parameters, runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and prints the system's time in a single line, for example '2020-06-29T22:29:37+00:00'. It reports the time based on the system configured timezone. For more detail use 'show clock current-time', which also gives universal-time, timezone, uptime, time-source, DST-active and last-time-jump, though show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond if DNS is not properly configured.

The 'uptime' command displays the system uptime and load average, for example '21:24:09 up 41 days, 15:56, 1 user, load average: 0.10, 0.35, 0.39'. The load average, also called average system load, indicates whether there are multiple tasks queued on the system (on the card). Whether it is high or low depends on the number of cores the system has, how many CPUs are integrated into the system (card), and the load average number itself. The rule to judge it: a load average value is considered high when it is greater than the number of CPUs on the card. The command takes no parameters and runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. 'manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<value>' takes the AID of the object to be switched, and the command warns before proceeding: 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. You confirm at that prompt to proceed with the manual switch operation, or pass -f to force the command without confirmation.
