Example AIDs by chassis: 'manual-switchover card-1-3' on a G42, 'manual-switchover card-1-5' on a G32, and 'manual-switchover card-1-12' on a G34c. Access: Operational mode. For the full procedure the guide refers to the 1830 GX Software Management Procedures Guide.

'show protection'. It takes no parameters and displays the node's protection container, that is the protection setting. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related objects underneath it have their own commands: 'show protection-group-<name>' for a group and its state and timers, and 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name>' for an individual member.

On protection-group, switching-mode defaults to unidirectional and accepts unidirectional or bidirectional. The wait-to-restore timer is wtr-timer: it is the trigger clearance soaking time before reverting to the working protection unit, measured and set in 1-second steps, range 60..720 seconds, default 300. It only applies in revertive mode, and reversion-mode itself defaults to non-revertive (values revertive, non-revertive), so you must set reversion-mode revertive for the WTR timer to take effect. The related read-only remaining-wtr shows the remaining WTR time in the range 0..720 seconds. The separate hold-off-timer is the switching trigger soaking time before switching, in 1-millisecond steps, range 0..10000 ms, default 0.

Use the operating command 'protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>'. For a force to the protection path: 'protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection'. operation-type takes force, lockout, manual or release; switch-target is the target of the switch command and is not needed for the release and lockout operations. -f forces the command without confirmation. Access: Operational mode. The equivalent configured request is the protection-group pg-request attribute, which accepts clear (the default), manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout and exercise (exercise applies only to bidirectional SNCP).

Use 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> [AID] [transport-entity] [state] [role] [alarm-report-control] [label]'. The state attribute is the one that tells you which member is carrying traffic: it takes active, standby, available or unknown. role tells you which member is which in the pair, taking working or protection. transport-entity gives the instance identifier of the underlying transport entity, and AID the object identifier. At group level, 'show protection-group-<name> pg-state' and last-switch-trigger show the switching state and what caused the last switchover. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Most alarms have both an automatic raise criteria and a clear criteria, but a very small subset have no clear criteria and instead require the user to acknowledge and clear them manually. Use 'clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [[resource=]<value>[,<value>]*]', for example 'clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL'; -f forces the command without confirmation. To find which alarms qualify, list the inventory entries that have can-be-cleared-by-user = true: 'show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true'. This mechanism applies only to system alarms that are not associated with any particular resource but with the system itself, that is system wide or global alarms. Access: Operational mode. To acknowledge rather than clear, use 'set-alarm-state ack ...'.

That is governed by arc-behavior on the alarm-control object, the system wide alarm-reporting-control behavior switch. It takes leave-alarms, which when ARC is set to inhibit leaves the current alarms in a raised mode, or clear-alarms, which when ARC is set to inhibit clears the current alarms. The default is leave-alarms, so by default the already-raised alarms stay up. Change it with 'set alarm-control arc-behavior clear-alarms' or 'set alarm-control arc-behavior leave-alarms', and check with 'show alarm-control'. The same object carries alarm-soaking-behavior, taking automatic (soaking time defined in the FM profile) or no-soak (certain alarms specified in the FM profile have no soaking time), default automatic. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Look it up in the alarm inventory, which holds all possible alarm types for the system with static information for each: 'show alarm-inventory-<alarm-type> [resource-type] [alarm-category] [alarm-type-description] [corrective-action] [default-severity] [service-affecting]', for example 'show alarm-inventory-TIM' or 'show alarm-inventory-MSIM'. alarm-type-description gives the description of the alarm type (string 0..128) and corrective-action gives system provided information on how to correct the situation that triggered it (string 0..256). alarm-category takes communication, facility, equipment, environmental, processing-error, software, quality-of-service or security. default-severity lists the possible default severities (critical, major, minor, warning, not-reported, event), which can differ by resource-type, and service-affecting takes indeterminate, sa, nsa or sa-nsa.

Yes, that is exactly what alarm-severity-entry is for: it configures the severity for one particular alarm. Use 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>'. resource-type is the type to be modified (for example CHM1R, FAN, 1830 GX G31), alarm-type is the abbreviated alarm code (for example ADMIN-LOCK, BERSD), direction is na, ingress or egress, and location is na, near-end or far-end. severity takes critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning. Examples: 'set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor' and 'set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major'. Read it back with the matching show, which also returns service-affecting. Press ? after the command to list the available entities. The object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted.

alarm-severity-entry addresses one specific alarm through the four-part key <resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>, for example 'set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor'. alarm-severity-profile instead sets the severity for an alarm profile entry: 'set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>', for example 'set alarm-severity-profile alarm-severity-entry-trusted-certificate/CERTIFICATE-EXPIRED severity critical'. Both take the same severity value set, and both objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Use 'show alarm-severity-profile' to view the profiles, and press ? after 'set alarm-severity-profile' to display the list of available profiles. Access for both: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'show current-alarms [number-of-alarms] [last-changed]'. number-of-alarms is the count of currently raised alarms, and last-changed is the timestamp of the last change in the current alarm list, covering either a raise or a clear event. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. For a breakdown by severity instead of a bare count, the System dashboard from the 'status' command includes an alarm summary giving the number of alarms per severity, for example '13 current alarms (1 critical, 5 major, 2 not-reported, 5 minor)'. The full list itself comes from 'show alarms'.

Look in the conditions with the 'get-conditions' command. A condition is an alarm that is not considered current, which happens when the alarm severity is configured as not-reported or not-alarmed, when the alarm is suppressed due to alarm correlation, when it is suppressed due to ARC (alarm reporting control), or when it is suppressed due to AINS. Syntax: 'get-conditions [[direction=]<value>] [[resource=]<value>] [[resource-type=]<value>] [[alarm-type=]<value>] [[location=]<value>] [[AID=]<value>]'. direction takes all, na, ingress or egress and defaults to all; location takes all, na, near-end or far-end and defaults to all; resource, resource-type, alarm-type and AID narrow the search further. Access: Operational mode.

Use the operational-mode command `set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>[,<value>]*)`. The state parameter is mandatory and takes an operator-state of 'none', 'ack' or 'close'. For a batch, either use the `all-alarms` option, which sets all currently raised alarms, or `alarm-id-list=` with a comma-separated list of from 1 up to 10 alarm ids. The optional `acknowledge-text` parameter inserts an acknowledge message stored in the alarm itself; it is a string of length 0..256. Setting an alarm to the state it already holds is accepted, with only the text being updated. Example: `set-alarm-state ack all-alarms acknowledge-text=example`, or `set-alarm-state ack 28872914984089790,17580406225060810165`.

Yes. The `statistics` command clears the event counters for specified objects: `clear [-f] statistics [target=]<value>[,<value>]*`, in Operational Mode. The `target` parameter is an instance-identifier naming the objects whose event counter statistics are cleared, and it accepts a comma-separated list. The `-f` flag forces the command without confirmation, and `-h` displays help. Scope is limited: currently the only supported object type is aaa-server, and AAA statistics are supported for TACACS+ servers but not for RADIUS servers. To clear all AAA servers use `clear statistics aaa-server`; to clear one server use `clear statistics aaa-server-MyServer`.

Use `show [-n=<number>] [-t] log [<logname> [exclude=<exclude-column> ...]]`. The `-n=x` flag limits the output to the last x entries and `-t` switches from the default CSV output to an aligned table display, so `show -n=5 -t log security` gives the last five security-log entries in readable columns. If the table becomes too wide, drop columns by adding `exclude=<column>` after the logname (use <tab> auto-complete to list the removable columns). Valid lognames are messages, linecard, shell-command, netconf-command, apps, cli-command, alarm, configuration, kernel, user, event, security and ztp; `show log` with no logname lists the available logs. You can also post-process with piped commands, for example `show log security | exclude john | include NETCONF`. Note that due to system restrictions the security log may not be cleared.

Yes, that is the default. The `log-console` object has an `enabled` attribute that switches console logging on and off, with permitted values true and false and a default of false, so nothing is logged to the console until you turn it on. Use `set log-console enabled true` and check with `show log-console`. The other attribute is `source-facilities`, the list of syslog facilities used in this configuration, whose values are all, authentication, clock-daemon-15, clock-daemon-9, ftp-daemon, kernel, line-printer, local1 through local7, log-alert, log-audit, mail-system, network-news, ntp, security, syslog-internal, system-daemons, user-level and uucp. Both set and show are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add a `log-console-facility-filter`, a selector that filters messages by source facility and severity: `add log-console-facility-filter-<name> [severity <value>] [compare-op <value>]`. The <name> identifies a single syslog facility, or all of them if the value is 'all'. `severity` takes emergency (0), alert (1), critical (2), error (3), warning (4), notice (5), informational (6) or debug (7), and defaults to informational. `compare-op` controls how the comparison is made: equals, equals-or-higher or not-equals, defaulting to equals-or-higher. So to suppress informational traffic and keep only serious messages, for example `add log-console-facility-filter-all severity 'critical'`, or use severity error with compare-op equals-or-higher. Use set to change an existing filter and `delete log-console-facility-filter-<name>` to remove it.

It is bounded by two `log-file` attributes. `max-file-size` is the maximum file size before rotation, in megabytes, with a range of 1..30 and a default of 30. `number-of-files` is the maximum number of log files retained, a uint8 with a range of 1..20 and a default of 10; when files are rotated because max-file-size has been reached, the oldest files are discarded if the total number of files exceeds number-of-files. So by default a log keeps ten files of up to 30 MB each and then starts discarding the oldest. Set them with `add log-file-<name> [number-of-files <value>] [max-file-size <value>]` or the equivalent `set`. Locally saved log files can be emptied with `clear` or removed with `delete`, but the default system log file cannot be edited or deleted.

Yes. First restrict the file's facilities: `add log-file-<name> source-facilities authentication` (the `source-facilities` attribute is the list of syslog facilities used in this configuration and defaults to all; 'authentication' is facility 4, used for authentication/authorization attempt messages). Then narrow by severity with a `log-file-facility-filter`, named as <log-file-name>/<log-file-facility-filter-name>, for example `add log-file-facility-filter-<name>/authentication severity error compare-op equals-or-higher`. The filter's severity values are emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notice, informational and debug, defaulting to informational, and compare-op is equals, equals-or-higher or not-equals, defaulting to equals-or-higher. The log-file name is a string of 0...128 characters and you can further constrain entries with `pattern-match`, a regex of length 0..255.

Configure a log-server: `add log-server-<name> address <IP address> ... port <value> transport <udp|tls|tcp>`. Unless you say otherwise the node uses port 514 (the `port` default; range 1..65535) and message format rfc5424 (the `message-format` default; the alternative is rfc3164). The `transport` default is udp, so for TLS you must set `transport tls` explicitly. Other defaults: `enabled` true, `message-coalescence` true, `origin` manual, `source-facilities` all, `sensitive-data` none, `destination-facility-override` disabled, `alarm-report-control` allowed. The server name is a string of 0...64 characters and `address` accepts IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS domain name. Example: `add log-server-1 address '10.220.225.165' source-facilities local7`.

Yes you can filter per collector, but no, it cannot widen what is sent. Use `add log-server-facility-filter-<log-server-name>/<log-server-facility-filter-name> [severity <value>] [compare-op <value>]`. The guide states this filter is based on the log-server's source-facilities leaf-list and can only add a filter to the configured source facilities, so it can only narrow the set already configured on that log-server. The filter name identifies a single syslog facility, or all of them if the value is 'all' (kernel, user-level, mail-system, system-daemons, authentication, syslog-internal, line-printer, network-news, uucp, clock-daemon-9, security, ftp-daemon, ntp, log-audit, log-alert, clock-daemon-15, local0 through local7, all). `severity` defaults to informational and `compare-op` to equals-or-higher, with equals and not-equals also allowed. Example: `add log-server-facility-filter-server184/local2 severity debug`.

Use the global `syslog` flag: `set syslog remote-logging-switch false`. The `remote-logging-switch` attribute takes true or false and defaults to true; when false it disables all remote logging destinations, leaving the configured log-server entries in place. A related flag is `log-relay`, true/false with a default of false, which when false disables all remote logging from a shelf controller to a node controller. Verify with `show syslog remote-logging-switch`. Both set and show are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Other syslog attributes include source-address (default localhost), log-file-message-coalescence (default true), assignment-method (both, manual or dhcp; default both), niap-compliant-logging (default false) and privacy-mode (default false).

The `shared-secret` attribute of `aaa-server` is documented as a string of length 0...128 with a default value of sharedkey, but the command note states that the maximum length of shared-secret is 64 characters and any value longer than 64 characters is denied with an error message. So 64 characters is the enforced limit. The value is displayed as * when shown. Set it with `add aaa-server-<server-name> ... [shared-secret <value>]` or `set aaa-server-<server-name> [shared-secret <value>]` in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. The server-name itself is a string of 1...64 characters.

No, that is expected behaviour. The `authentication-requests` counter shown by `show aaa-statistics-<server-name>` displays the number of authentication requests, and the guide notes that for TACACS+ the default authentication protocol includes both PAP and CHAP. The counter tracks each retry and each authentication protocol attempted independently, so authentication requests may increase by 2 for each retry. The other counters available on `show aaa-statistics-<server-name>` are connection-failures (which includes failures due to unavailable servers and timeouts), authentication-rejects, authorization-requests, authorization-rejects and accounting-requests, all integers. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, and applies to AAA servers using the TACACS+ protocol.

If you omit `action` on `add ace-<name>/<sequence-id>`, the default is drop; the other permitted values are accept and reject. An ACL must be in place before an ACE can be added, and to add an ACE at least one of Source IP, Destination IP, L4 ports, TTL or protocol must be provided. The number of rules is bounded by the sequence-id range, which is 1-100 for AUX and DCN-B interfaces and 1-256 for the DCN-A interface; multiples of 5 are recommended so rules can be inserted later. In addition, a maximum of 16 ACEs can be created on an ACL if both upper-port and lower-port values are specified, and attempting to add a 17th such ACE returns an error. Other defaults: direction input, protocol any, logging-action false, ttl 255, source/destination lower and upper ports 0.

An ACL is bound to one management interface at creation: `add acl-<name> type <value> interface <value> [admin-state <value>]`. The available interfaces are 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2 and DCN-2-B (use `add acl-name interface ?` to list them). An ACL can be added on the DCN-B interface when the DCN is operating in active-active configuration. Yes, IPv6 is handled: the `type` parameter indicates the top-level type of ACL, that is which fields from the associated IPv4 or IPv6 headers the ACL matches on, and its permitted values are IPv4 and IPv6, with no default, so it must be given on add. The ACL name is a string of 0...30 characters and `admin-state` takes lock, maintenance or unlock, defaulting to unlock. Example: `add acl-AuxV4traffic interface 1-AUX-2 type ipv4`.

Yes. `show access-control-list` displays the access control list. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the individual objects behind it, use `show acl-<name> [admin-state] [oper-state] [avail-state] [type] [interface]` for a specific access control list and `show ace-<name>/<sequence-id> [label] [direction] [logging-action] [source-ip-address] [source-lower-port] [source-upper-port] [destination-ip-address] [destination-lower-port] [destination-upper-port] [ttl] [action] [protocol]` for the individual access control entries within it.

Create an access-rule-list bound to that group, then add a deny rule to it. First `add access-rule-list-<name> [user-group <value>]`, where user-group is a leaf-list of user-group names (default '*' meaning all groups, maximum 20 groups referenced). Then `add access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> action deny [path <value>] [operation <value>] [module-name <value>] [attribute <value>] [attribute-value <value>] [sequence-id <value>] [description <value>]`. `action` is mandatory and takes permit or deny. `path` is the target object, an XPath of a YANG data node, notification, RPC or descendant, or an external command, max 255 characters, default '*'. `operation` is a bits value from create, read, update, delete, execute, default '*'. Example: `add access-rule-1/rule path /ne/equipment/card operation create action deny`. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists.

Order is by `sequence-id`: the access-rule-list is processed in order as given by the sequence-id parameter, and lower number ids are processed first, so the lowest sequence-id wins. It is a uint16, and if not provided it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, placing the entry at the end of the list; you can change it over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries. The same sequence-id rule applies to the individual access-rules within a list. To say which groups a list applies to, use the `user-group` parameter: `add access-rule-list-<name> [user-group <value>] [sequence-id <value>] [description <value>]`. It is a leaf-list of user-group names, or '*' as the match-all default meaning the list applies to all existing user-groups, and a maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. Example: `add access-rule-list-A user-group XY`.

Despite the generic name, `auth-key` is OSPFv3-specific: it adds, edits or shows the pre-shared key used for OSPFv3 IPsec integrity protection. The instance is keyed entirely by OSPF identifiers: `add auth-key-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> key <value> [type <value>]`, where instance-id is the OSPF instance ID (number, range 0..255), ospf-area-id is the OSPF Router Area ID (string), ospf-if-name is a reference to the interface in the OSPF area (string), and spi is a unique security parameter index for the SA (number, range 256..4294967295). `key` is a string of length 8..128, and `type` indicates whether the integrity key is ascii or hex encoded. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add auth-key-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 key abcdefgh12345678`.

Set the global authorization mode to rules-only: `set authorization mode rules-only`. The `mode` attribute selects which authorization rules are used and takes static-only (only system defined static rules), static+rules (both user and system rules, with a user configured access-rule matched first and system rules as fallback) or rules-only (only user defined access-rules; if no rule matches, the global defaults apply). The default mode is static+rules. In rules-only mode the fallbacks are `read-default` (default permit), `write-default` (default deny) and `exec-default` (default permit), each permit or deny, and they are only configurable when mode = rules-only. To deny anything the rules do not cover, set all three to deny, for example `set authorization write-default deny`. `show authorization` also reports denied-operations, denied-data-writes and denied-notifications, counted since the last system restart.

Every user changes their own password with the Operational mode `password [old-password=<old-password>] [new-password=<new-password>]` command. Both the current/old and the new password are required, and this is supported only for local users. A password may contain up to 200 characters. Input can be inline as normal parameters (not hidden from view, usable in scripts) or interactively, where the passwords are prompted for, not echoed, and the new one must be typed twice to confirm; Ctrl+C cancels. Inline, the special characters \" and ' must be escaped with \ and #?|; must be enclosed in single or double quotes. For resetting another user's password, an administrator uses `set user-<username> force-password-change true`, which forces that user to change their password on next login; the underlying `force-password-change` attribute is true/false with a default of false.

`show security` displays the top level security container. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. From there, related commands cover the individual pieces: `show security-policies` for the system security policy flags (secure-mode, strict-password-check, minimum-password-length, SSH and TLS algorithm lists, and so on), `show access-control-list` for access control lists, `show authorization` for the authorization mode and defaults, `show user-<user-name>` and `show user-group-<name>` for users and groups, and `show user-data`.

Both are `security-policies` attributes. `minimum-password-length` is the configurable minimum length for user passwords, a number in the range 1..200 with a default of 8; the length is verified against this policy whenever a password is changed. Related to it, `strict-password-check` (true/false, default true) enforces a minimum length of 8 characters plus at least one lower case letter, one upper case letter, one number and one symbol, and forbids the user name being part of the password; if disabled, only a minimum length of 1 character applies. For history, `enforce-password-history-check` (true/false, default true) ensures a new password cannot match any of the previous 5 passwords for that user, and `password-history-size` sets the number of passwords stored for reuse checking, a number in the range 1..200 with a default of 5. Both policies only affect newly defined passwords once enabled.

These are per-user attributes of the `user` command. `max-invalid-login` is the maximum number of consecutive invalid login attempts before an account is suspended (locked out); it is a number in the range 0-255 with a default of 5. `suspension-time` is the duration of UID suspension following those consecutive invalid login attempts, in minutes, range 0 - 1440, default 5. Set them with `add user-<user-name> [max-invalid-login <value>] [suspension-time <value>]` or the equivalent `set`. `show user-<user-name>` also reports `failed-logins`, the number of previous failed logins, which resets to zero upon a successful login, and `user-status`, which reads 'lockout' when the account is locked out due to unsuccessful login attempts. Lockout can be turned off globally with the `disable-user-lockout` attribute of security-policies.

`show user-data` displays the user-data. The command takes no parameters and is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode; show is the only verb. For per-user detail use `show user-<user-name>` instead, which returns password, password-hashed, user-group, display-name, max-invalid-login, suspension-time, timeout, password-aging-interval, password-expiration-date, enabled, user-status, force-password-change, max-sessions, last-login-date, failed-logins, user-aaa-type, alarm-report-control and label.

Use `add user-group-<name> [description <value>]` in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. The group `name` is a string of 1...64 characters and `description`, the long description of the user group, is a string of 1...128 characters. Each user is associated with a list of groups and derives its permissions from them, assigned via the `user-group` attribute of the user command. Use `set user-group-<name> [description <value>]` to edit, `show user-group` to list all groups with their descriptions, and `delete user-group-<name>` to remove one. The system already ships with EA (Encryption Administrator), MA (Monitoring Access), NA (Network Administrator), NE (Network Engineer), PR (Provisioning), SA (Security Administrator) and TT (Turn-up and Test). Example: `add user-group-XY`.

Add/Drop Groups are keyed by adg-number, an integer in the range [1..110]. Manage them with add adg-<adg-number>, set adg-<adg-number> [label <value>], delete adg-<adg-number>, and show adg-<adg-number> [label] [max-add-drop-ports] [wavelength-duplication] [bands-supported]; access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Duplication is reported by the read-only wavelength-duplication attribute, default one-per-adg, meaning no duplication of frequencies in the ADG. The other value is one-per-degree: CDC operation, where duplication of frequencies is allowed in the ADG but only one at the Degree. Only CDCs allow more than one instance of the same wavelength on the ADG. label is a String of length 0..256, and bands-supported defaults to standardC-band.

On set amplifier-<name>, gain-target sets the constant-gain value over 0..40 dB, default 0.0, and it applies only when control-mode is manual. control-mode is auto-max-pw (default, auto mode targeting maximum output power) or manual; amp-control-support says whether auto-max-pw is permitted (auto) or manual-only. In auto mode you bias the system value with gain-adjustment, range [-20.00..20.00], default 0, supported only on amplifiers with function pa or inline. gain-operating reports the actually configured gain (0.0 when the card is out or the EDFA is disabled). Tilt is controlled by tilt-control-mode: auto (default, system controls tilt per configured fiber parameters), auto-planned (per planning tool parameters), or manual. So yes, tilt is automatic by default. Manual mode uses tilt-target [-5..5] dB, default 0dB, and auto/auto-planned use tilt-adjustment [-5..5] dB, default 0dB. When amplifier function is add or drop the only option is manual. Changing tilt-target raises the warning that the attribute may be traffic affecting.

Use set amplifier-raman-<name> target-raman-gain <value>. The range is [0, 5..30dB] with default 0dB. It is configurable only when control-mode is different than auto; in auto the parameter is ignored. control-mode values are auto (you configure only the span attributes and optionally pointloss, gain is controlled automatically), auto-planned (you configure the target Raman gain plus span attributes), and manual (basic manual configuration where even the amplifier target pump powers must be configured); default is auto. Pump count comes from the read-only number-of-pumps attribute in show amplifier-raman-<name>: values are 4 or 2, for the required-equipped card, and that value dictates the number of pump-power objects the system exposes. total-pump-power reports the operating total pump power, range [-99..99 dBm], where -99 means no power or card not actual.

Switch it on with set ase-idler-service-<name> ase-idler-enable enabled, for example set ase-idler-service-1-8 ase-idler-enable enabled. The attribute takes enabled or disabled and defaults to disabled; enabled turns on ASE idler signal filling on the unused and nmc-failed portions of the band spectrum. ase-idler-enable can also be given on add ase-idler-service-<name>, alongside alarm-report-control (allowed, default, or inhibited). To see whether it actually came up, read the read-only ase-idler-state with show ase-idler-service-<name> ase-idler-state: ase-enabled (filling complete on the band spectrum), ase-partially-enabled (filling incomplete), ase-faulted (ASE idler signal is faulted), or ase-disabled (signal completely removed), with ase-disabled the default. oper-state (enabled/disabled) and avail-state are also shown. The function attribute is idler.

Use set ase-idler-source-<name> target-output-power <value>. That attribute is the ASE pump output power required when manually configured, with range (-3.00..20.50) dBm and default 13. The pump is not on by default: pump-enable takes enabled or disabled and defaults to disabled, so you must set it explicitly. The read-only pump-state reports the actual state of the ASE Idler pump, also enabled/disabled with default disabled. A combined example is set ase-idler-source-1-3.1-ase pump-enable 'enabled' target-output-power '15.00'. Other settable attributes are admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), label (0..256 chars) and alarm-report-control (allowed, default, or inhibited). function is fixed at ase-idler-source.

Use the calibrate command in Operational Mode. The syntax is calibrate [type=]<value> [trigger=]<value> [entity=]<value>. type currently only takes raman, which triggers calibration on raman cards. trigger takes start, which starts the Raman gain calibration for the OTS span, or stop, which stops it. entity selects the object to be calibrated as an instance-identifier; for raman calibration the entity may be an OTS-R entity. To start: calibrate raman start ots-r-1-1-dwdm-line. To stop: calibrate raman stop ots-r-1-1-dwdm-line. None of the three parameters has a default, so all must be supplied.

A degree is keyed by degree-number, an integer in the range [1..20], and it must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. Use add degree-<degree-number> [label <value>], delete degree-<degree-number>, set degree-<degree-number> [label <value>], and show degree-<degree-number> [label] [is-foadm] [wss-less] [slot-width-granularity] [center-freq-granularity] [min-slots] [max-slots] [bands-supported]. Spectral granularity is read-only: slot-width-granularity is the width of a slot, default 6250 MHz, and center-freq-granularity is the granularity of allowed center frequencies, default 3125 MHz, computed from a base frequency of 193.1 THz per G.694.1. min-slots (default 8) and max-slots (default 32) bound how many slots may be joined to form a media channel; min-slots must be less than or equal to max-slots. bands-supported defaults to standardC-band.

On a multi-rail ILA node the system pairs the indexes to the two line ports of one card. Direction n and direction n+1 are automatically assigned by the system to the DWDM Line1 and DWDM Line2 ports of the #n C2ILASGH/D2ILASGM card created, where index n is an odd integer with a value between 1 and 15. DWDM Line1 is always assigned an odd index value and DWDM Line2 always an even index value. The index range is [1..16] (1 and 2 are used when migrating from R6.x). The system-set direction-number follows: 1 when direction-port is dwdm-line1, 2 when it is dwdm-line2, default 1. So dwdm-line port instances for an odd index should be dwdm-line1 and for an even index dwdm-line2. The same dwdm-line* port instance of an ILAx can only be selected once per NE. direction-card is filled in autonomously as card-<chassis>-<slot>. Create with add direction-<index> direction-port <value> [label <value>]; delete [-f] forces without confirmation.

The dsc commands are add, delete, set and show, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. On add dsc-<name> and set dsc-<name> you can configure just three attributes: label (String, length 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock or maintenance, default unlock), and alarm-report-control (allowed, the default, or inhibited). Everything else is read-only: supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, supported-facilities, AID, oper-state (enabled/disabled, default disabled), avail-state and managed-by. managed-by describes whether this facility was system created or not; its values are system and user, with default system. The practical consequence is that only user-created facilities can be user deleted, so a dsc showing managed-by system cannot be deleted by you.

On add dsc-group-<name> or set dsc-group-<name> there are four Q-related attributes. pre-fec-q-sig-deg-threshold is the threshold that raises the PRE-FEC-Q-SIGNAL-DEGRADE alarm: decimal64 with 3 fraction digits, range 0|5.600..9.600 dB, where 0 disables threshold crossing alarming and the specific sub-range is per carrier use-case. pre-fec-q-sig-deg-hysteresis accounts for raising that alarm: decimal64, 1 fraction digit, range 0.1..1.0 dB, default 0.5. post-fec-q-sig-deg-threshold raises POST-FEC-Q-SIGNAL-DEGRADE: decimal64, 1 fraction digit, range 12.5..18.0 dB, default 18. post-fec-q-sig-deg-hysteresis is decimal64, 1 fraction digit, range 0.1..1.0 dB, default 0.5. Alongside them, dgd-high-threshold raises DGD-OORH: uint16, range 25..400 ps, default 100.

Use the gadt command, which retrieves golden carrier application information. The syntax is show gadt [<application-description-H|application-description-P|application-description-S|application-description-U>], available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Each of the four parameters is a detailed description of an application ID and is returned as a string; there are no defaults. For example, show gadt application-description-H returns application-description 'Subsea modes using Uniform and Hybrid modulation'. Running show gadt with no parameter lists them all. The application ID letter also appears as the application field in golden-carrier-mode and gcmt output.

gapt lists the golden advanced parameters from the Golden Advanced Parameters Table (GAPT). The syntax is show gapt-<card-type> [version] [applicable-resource-type], in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, so the scoping key is the card type: card-type is a string naming the card type, giving one GAPT instance per card type such as gapt-CHM6, gapt-CHM7, gapt-CHM7T. version is the table version, a string of length 0..5 (for example 1.8 for CHM6, 3.0 for CHM7). applicable-resource-type is a string naming the managed resource type(s) applicable for that particular advanced parameter. show gapt with no key lists every table with its version; show gapt-chm7 lists that card type's entries, named golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/<parameter>, for example golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/NLC and golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/RxCDMode.

Use the gcmt command, which retrieves information about the golden carrier mode. The syntax is show gcmt [<card-type>] [version], in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and you pass the mode instance directly: show gcmt golden-carrier-mode-800M.95P. The output row is keyed by the fully qualified name including card type, for example golden-carrier-mode-CHM6/800M.95P, and reports capacity (Gbps) 800, client-mode ethernet-otn, baud-rate (GBaud) 95.2965203, application P, compatibility-id 6, and status supported. The version parameter shows the table version. For the full attribute set of one mode, including actual-carrier-mode, sop-tracking-mode, supported-subtypes and candidate-subtypes, use show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode>.

Read the status attribute, which describes the carrier mode release status. Its values are supported, candidate, experimental, deprecated and diagnostic. Retrieve it with show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode> [status], for example alongside [actual-carrier-mode] [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [sop-tracking-mode] [supported-subtypes] [candidate-subtypes]; access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. status also appears as a column in show gcmt output. Related fields: supported-subtypes lists the subtypes each carrier mode supports (string 0..32, maximum 20 elements) and candidate-subtypes lists subtypes for which this carrier mode has candidate status (string 0..16, maximum 10 elements). carrier-mode itself is a string of 1..15 formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, for example 600E.84P.

Use l0-capabilities. The command shows the capabilities details related with the node's Layer 0 functions. The syntax is simply show l0-capabilities, and it takes no parameters. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. For the OADM-specific limits use show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs].

Creation requires three mandatory arguments: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value>, plus optional [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [auto-delete <value>]. parent-oms is an instance-identifier set only upon MC creation, and its referenced supporting-card must be part of a Degree and cannot be in an ADG. lower-frequency and upper-frequency are values in MHz. The system derives center-frequency (in MHz) and slot-width from upper-frequency minus lower-frequency; both are show-only. Example: add mc-1-3.1-dwdm-line-192262500 parent-oms '1-3.1-dwdm-line' lower-frequency '192225000' upper-frequency '192300000'. auto-delete defaults to disabled; enabling it lets the system delete the MC when its NMC is deleted, and it is only allowed on RD66TM sleds (l0-mode-op=hsc-ols), always disabled if l0-mode-op is standard or slte.

The Media Channel Filler is read only. The mc-f command supports show only: show mc-f-<name> [supporting-facilities] [supported-facilities] [supporting-card] [supporting-port] [AID] [lower-frequency] [upper-frequency] [slot-width]. Every parameter is used in show and none has a configurable default. lower-frequency and upper-frequency are the lower and upper frequency of the MC Filler in MHz units, and slot-width is calculated by the system from upper-frequency minus lower-frequency. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. By contrast the Network Media Channel Filler, nmc-f, does allow set nmc-f-<name> [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>].

Up to four. In add modules-adg-<adg-number>/<index> supported-card <value> [ocm-monitoring <value>], adg-number is a number in the range [1..110] and index is a number in the range [1..4], where index identifies the card within the ADG that is fibered to the degree. The card with index 1 must be the card, subcard or module fibered to the Degree(s). supported-card is the instance identifier of the card, for example add modules-adg-1/1 supported-card card-1-6. Channel monitoring is on by default: ocm-monitoring defaults to true. It is set upon creation and cannot be changed after supported-card has been assigned, but it can optionally be configured to false for OMD cards directly connected to PAx/BAX or C2ILASGH degrees, for example on FOADM nodes. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, for Network Administrator and Network Engineer.

Use modules-degree: add modules-degree-<degree-number>/<index> supported-card <value>, for example add modules-degree-1/1 supported-card card-1-1. degree-number is a number in the range [1..20] and must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. index is restricted to the single value 1; the card with index 1 must be the card, subcard or module fibered to the Degree(s). supported-card is the instance identifier of the card or subcard that belongs to the degree, and in R6.0 the card must be RD09SM or RD20TM. The companion commands are set modules-degree-<degree-number>/<index> [supported-card <value>], show modules-degree-<degree-number>/<index> [supported-card] and delete modules-degree-<degree-number>/<index>. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, for Network Administrator and Network Engineer.

Use show monitored-channel-<name>/<frequency> monitored-optical-power, for example show monitored-channel-1-1.2-ocm1-in/195987500 monitored-optical-power. The entity is keyed by two parts: name, which corresponds to the (WS04S) card name with the suffix -1 or -2 for ocm1-in or ocm2-in respectively, and frequency, the nominal center frequency of the carrier in MHz (uint32). monitored-optical-power is the measured power for that carrier in dBm, decimal64 with range (-99.00..99.00) and default -99, where -99.00 means no power. The other readable attribute is monitored-width, the carrier width configured at the NMC within the oxcon source/destination, in MHz (uint32, default 0). The command is show only, in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode; omitting the attribute name shows all attributes of that channel.

On add nmc-<name> parent-facility <value> center-frequency <value> [width <value>], center-frequency is the nominal center frequency of the NMC and takes values in the range [190650000..196700000] MHz. width is the Network Media Channel frequency width in MHz, values in the range [15000..200000] MHz, default 35000. You must configure the 3 dB signal bandwidth: the value in GHz must be equivalent to the baud rate in GBd configured on the connected transponder line interface line port. Both center-frequency and width are set only at add time (used in add and show, not set). parent-facility can be either a Media Channel or an OMS and is only set upon creation, and its referenced supporting-card must be part of a Degree and cannot be in an ADG. Example: add nmc-cdc-1-4_192800000-34000 center-frequency 192800000 width 34000 parent-facility oms-1-4-ad1.

The Network Media Channel Filler occupies 75000 MHz by default: alloc-bandwidth, the allocated bandwidth of the NMC Filler, is a value in MHz units with default 75000. The companion alloc-lower-frequency and alloc-upper-frequency give the allocated band edges in MHz. The actually occupied span is reported separately by actual-lower-frequency, actual-upper-frequency and actual-bandwidth, the last defaulting to 0 MHz. Yes, it is monitored: monitoring-state indicates whether the NMC is intended to be in use and, because this is a system created attribute, it is enabled by default (values enabled/disabled). Power readings power-actual-tx and power-actual-rx are in the range [-99.00..99.00] dBm with default -99. All of these are show-only; the only settable attributes are admin-state and alarm-report-control via set nmc-f-<name>.

Use show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs], available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. max-degrees is the maximum number of degrees, reported as 20 (uint8), and 0 if not supported. Degrees are only supported in OADM node types; the maximum degrees for the ILA node-type is 0 by convention, because an ILA has only 2 directions, fixedly, and this is not shown in supported capabilities. Note that the maximum number of Degrees is not necessarily the deployment supported configuration, but the maximum number of a working degree-number. max-adgs is the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups, reported as 110 (uint8), and 0 if not supported; ADGs are only supported in OADM node types. Typical output is max-degrees 20 and max-adgs 110.

On set oc-<name>, loopback selects the loopback mode and takes facility, terminal or none, default none; it is useful to debug on the fiber connection. loopback-mode indicates the loopback action for facility or terminal and takes facility or terminal, with no default. For test patterns, test-signal-type is the type of test pattern that is injected and takes none, enumeration, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9 or PRBS31, default none. test-signal-direction is the direction of the test signal and only takes ingress, which is also the default. test-signal-monitoring monitors the incoming test signals for diagnostics and takes true or false, default false, for example set oc-1-5-T9.1 test-signal-monitoring false. All of these are readable through show oc-<name>. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

It comes from the OSC. In ILA nodes the OCHm represents the signaled optical channel from OSC, detected at the ILA OMS by using the OSC information. Consequently, when either the OMS monitoring-mode is not-monitored (as configured by the user) or there is no OSC messaging information, the list of OCHm facilities in the NE will be empty. Read them with show ochm-<name> [supporting-card] [supporting-port] [AID] [admin-state] [oper-state] [avail-state] [managed-by] [direction] [power-actual] [target-actual-power] [attenuation-actual]. direction supports ingress and egress but currently only egress is supported (the default). power-actual is the currently received power in dBm, default -99, where -99 dBm means the power is not yet measured (measurement is performed by the OCM at the DGE2 card) or no power is detected or there is no appropriate fiber-connection; for egress it should be calibrated at the DWDM Line port output. Settable attributes are label, admin-state and alarm-report-control.

Use `show ocm-channel-<name>/<lower-frequency>/<upper-frequency>`. The ocm-channel object lists the detected carriers within the configured OXcon(s); it is show-only, in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The key is the entity name (String, length 0..64) plus lower-frequency and upper-frequency (uint32), which bound the spectrum slice of the corresponding OPM-pwr point. The displayable values are opm-pwr, the Optical Parameter Monitor power in dBm, decimal64 range -99.00..99.00 with default -99, and connected, true or false with default false, which yields true if that channel is configured, that is, involved in an oxcon.

Yes at a monitoring point. On `ocm-mp` the attribute ocm-enable, which enables regular power monitoring, takes disabled or enabled and defaults to enabled. Change it with `set ocm-mp-<name> ocm-enable <value>`; the only other settable attributes are label (String 0..256) and admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock). Related read-only state: monitoring-state, which the system reports as enabled when an OMS reference exists (default enabled); monitored-port, which can differ from supporting-port for a non-integrated OCM (default not-applicable); and ad-direction, which on an ocm-mp is ingress only. Note the sibling ocm-ptp facility defaults ocm-enable to disabled instead.

Dedicated OCM monitoring comes from the `ocm-ptp` facility, which is available for WS04S cards within a CD-AD ADG. It is not on out of the box: ocm-enable takes enabled or disabled and defaults to disabled, so you must run for example `set ocm-ptp-1-1.2-ocm1-in ocm-enable enabled`. Settable attributes are label, admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock) and ocm-enable. Read-only: ad-direction (egress or ingress, default ingress), last-measurement (date-and-time or never, default never), adg-number (uint8, range 0..110, default 0) and monitoring-state (default disabled), which the system reports as enabled only when complete connectivity at the AD is established and OCM measurement is possible.

An OMS defaults to grid-mode flexible, which lets you create and delete MCs of different widths. The other values are fixed-50G-96ch, fixed-100G-48ch, fixed-75G-64ch, fixed-75G-64ch-oif, fixed-50G-7100 (50GHz, 88 channels, set automatically when osc-compatibility is osc-7100) and fixed-150G-40ch. Default spectrum edges are lower-frequency 191300000 and upper-frequency 196150000 (standardC-band). monitoring-mode selects how the section is monitored: not-monitored (non-intrusive, no OCM/DGE required), intrusive (TTP), non-intrusive (CTP, operates with OCM such as DGE), dge-fixed-attenuation, ila-with-equalization (DGE plus OCM) and integrated-equalization. Default is intrusive for all node types except ILA, not-monitored for ILA, and integrated-equalization for hyperscale ILA nodes. It is only exposed for an OMS of a port belonging to a degree, or on an ILA node.

`set ops-<name>` accepts label (String 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed), input-psd-profile, role and port-expansion. input-psd-profile is the nominal expected tributary channel power density in dBm/12.5GHz, decimal64 range -30..-6, default -6. role is tributary (single add/drop to a local or remote transponder), multi-carrier (multiple carriers on the underlying filter port), general-purpose (the default, for express cross-connection to another filter), ase-input (only on specific RD ports, in SLTE l0-mode-op) or active-multi-carrier (port has active control). supported-roles is read-only and exposes which roles the card, and sometimes the card-mode, permits. port-expansion is no (default) or y-cable. Example: `set ops-1-6-ad1 role tributary`.

On `optical-carrier`, frequency is the center frequency the carrier is tuned to, range 0 | 191275000..196125000 MHz, where 0 means not configured; the usable sub-range and step depend on module and pluggable, for example CHM2TX 191292500-196137500 MHz (step 1 MHz), CHM7 and CHM7X 190625000-196725000 MHz (step 50 MHz), CHM6 191333000-196117000 MHz, TOM-400G-C-DWDM 191275000-196125000 MHz. Yes, you can trim it: frequency-offset provides bright tuning, int16 range -6000..6000 MHz, default 0; once set the frequency changes slowly over 1-10 s without affecting service. tx-power is the transmit power into the fiber, range -55.0..55.00 dBm adjustable in 0.5 dBm steps, bounded per module: CHM2TX -6 to 0 (default 0), CHM7/CHM7X -10 to 0 (default -2), UTM2 default -6.0, TOM-400G-C-DWDM -10 to +1 (default 1).

Yes. On `optical-carrier` set propagate-shutdown to enabled: the transmit laser is shut down if the whole service of that direction has signal failure. The function is mainly used at a regeneration node to propagate signal failure as LOS. Values are enabled and disabled, with default disabled. Pair it with propagate-shutdown-holdoff-timer, the hold off time of propagate shutdown, range 0..2000 milliseconds, default 0. Restriction: neither propagate-shutdown nor propagate-shutdown-holdoff-timer is configurable on the SPN2 or SPN2C card. Both are set and show attributes, used as `set optical-carrier-<name> propagate-shutdown enabled`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Very little. `set optical-channel-<name>` accepts only two attributes: label, a user-defined string of length 0..256, and admin-state, which takes lock, unlock or maintenance and defaults to unlock, for example `set optical-channel-channel1 admin-state unlock`. Everything else on the object is read-only through `show optical-channel-<name>`: supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, supported-facilities, AID (String 1..64), oper-state (enabled or disabled, default disabled), avail-state, and managed-by (system or user, default system, and only user-created facilities can be user deleted). Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show optical-ptp-<name> laser-state`. laser-state is read-only and reports the emitting pump (for example booster) laser state as enabled or disabled, default disabled; it is only of relevance for DWDM line ports. On RD amplifiers it reflects the source (Tx) pump; on Raman modules the pump laser. Yes, you can add fixed pad on receive: fix-rx-attenuation is a settable fixed attenuator before port Rx, decimal64 with 2 fraction digits, range 0..30 dB, default 0, where 0 dB means no fixed attenuator, for example `set -f optical-ptp-1-6-dwdm fix-rx-attenuation 10`. fix-tx-attenuation has the same range but is only visible when ops.port-expansion=y-cable. Measured levels are power-actual-rx and power-actual-tx, -99.00..99.00 dBm.

On `optical-switch` the Signal Fail (LOS) thresholds are working-los-threshold and protection-los-threshold. Both are settable in dBm, range -55.0 to 0 dBm, default -23 dBm, so by default a path is declared failed below -23 dBm. los-threshold-hysteresis is the SF threshold hysteresis, decimal64 range 0.5 to 5.0 dB in 0.1 dB steps, default 3 dB, with 1 dB recommended for MCHP and OMSP deployments. Separately, facility-los-threshold sets the facility port level below which loss of signal occurs, range -55 to 15 dBm, default -30.0 dBm. Signal Degrade uses working-switch-threshold and protection-switch-threshold, same -55.0 to 0 dBm range, default -18 dBm, and they act only when switch-threshold-enable is enabled (default disabled).

`set osc-<name>` accepts label, admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed), l0-comm-interface-type (ipv4 or ipv6; ipv4 for standard OLS, ipv6 for SLTE and HSC OLS), osc-control (auto or manual, default auto; only manual in R6.0, auto from R6.0.1, and HSC OLS nodes support auto only), target-output-power, the OSC Tx power defined at the DWDM line port output, na or -2.5..4.5 dBm, default na, tx-power-adjustment, an adjustment to the automatically calculated Tx target, na or -6..6 dB, default 0, voa-attenuation-target-rx, the Rx VOA target for manual control mode, 0..30 dB, default 10, and lof-soak-timer, short (default, about 3 ms) or long (adds 18,400 OC-3 frames, about 2300 ms), applicable only to the PBAx card.

Use `show otdr-<name> otdr-state`. otdr-state indicates the current status of the OTDR and a status change triggers a change notification: not-available (status not available, the default), idle, measuring (measurement is ongoing), finished (measurement has completed) or fail (measurement has failed). When it reads fail, otdr-error carries the error message produced when the measurement ends with error. Supporting read-only fields are otdr-measurement-time, the time remaining in the current measurement (default 0), otdr-laser-state (not-available, enabled, disabled), otdr-measurement-port where 0 means the card is not measuring any port, otdr-measurement-direction (not-available, tx, rx) and otdr-ongoing-measurement-profile (none, short, medium, long, raman-precheck1, raman-precheck2, raman-precheck3).

On `otdr-ptp`: otdr-range is the distance range in kilometres used to calculate the measurement repetition period, auto (default) or 0...300.0 km; it is recommended to set the actual fibre length plus 10 percent, and from R9.1 auto is derived from the OTS fiber-length-tx/fiber-length-rx with 10 percent margin, rounded up to the nearest 10 km. otdr-resolution is the data sampling resolution, auto (default) or 0.4...100.0. otdr-pulse-width is auto or 10...20,000 ns. otdr-measurement-speed is fast (about 10 s), medium (15 s), slow (1 minute), precision (3 to 5 minutes), high-precision (5 to 7 minutes) or auto (default). Also settable: otdr-ior (auto or 1.0...2.0), peak-power (auto or 5...14.5) and launching-fiber-length, 0...50 m, default 0, with auto not supported.

On the `ots` facility. fiber-type-tx and fiber-type-rx declare the fibre, from AllWave, DrakaLL, DSF, LEAF, LS, PSLC, PureSilica, SMF-ULL, SSMF, Teralight, TWC, TWMinus, TWPlus, TWReach, TWRS and VistaCor, default SSMF. fiber-length-tx and fiber-length-rx are auto (default) or 0..500.0 km, and are required for tilt control and when Raman backward pumping is deployed. Fibre loss goes in span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive, decimal64 range 0..80 dB (0..80, 99 dB on receive), default 0; these are the fibre loss only, so extra loss such as a patch panel goes in external-attenuation-tx and external-attenuation-rx, 0..30 dB, default 0. span-loss-reference chooses configured or measured, default measured. Changing span-loss-receive is traffic affecting. span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0.00..10.00 dB, default 1.0.

The ots-diagnostics name is auto generated by the system on line card provisioning, so you never create the object. The format is ots-diagnostics-<chassis>-<slot>-<DWDM Line>, and the name attribute itself is shown as <chassis>-<slot>-<DWDM Line>. An RD20TM DWDM line therefore gives `show ots-diagnostics-1-1-dwdm-line`, and a C2ILASGH with two lines gives ots-diagnostics-1-1-dwdm-line1 and ots-diagnostics-1-1-dwdm-line2. Only two attributes are settable: nmoper-alarm-reporting (disabled or enabled, default disabled; when enabled a mismatch between expected-operator and rx-operator raises the NMOPER alarm) and expected-operator (up to 32 characters). tx-operator is automatically defaulted by the system with the format <ne-name>-<Dxx>, that is <ne-name>-D00.

`ots-r` is the Optical Transport Section with reduced scope. Its required-fiber-type-rx, the required fibre type on the DWDM Line with reference to the Rx fibre, defaults to SSMF; the other choices are AllWave, DrakaLL, DSF, LEAF, LS, PSLC, PureSilica, SMF-ULL, Teralight, TWC, TWMinus, TWPlus, TWReach, TWRS and VistaCor. It is only of relevance if control-mode = auto and when there is no fiber-connection. About the receive span you can also set fiber-length-rx (unspecified by default, or 0..500.0), span-loss-receive (span-loss-info, default 99), external-attenuation-rx, target-power-setting (manual or auto, default auto) and delta-pointloss, additional Rx attenuation determined after turning up pumps, not-applicable by default or -1..3.5 dB. Read-only: configured-fiber-type-rx, configured-fiber-length-rx, span-loss-at-amplifier, power-actual-rx and connected-reference.

Yes, and the default does depend on the deployment. The `ots-r-auto-otdr` entity, added on an ots-r container, carries automatic-otdr (enabled or disabled), which enables OTDR based automatic fibre check. The default is enabled for green field deployments and disabled for in-field SW upgrade; it is also enabled by default if the Raman card is associated with a base card equipped with integrated OTDR, and disabled if the NE has a Raman card that is not aggregated with the EDFA card. The setting persists over warm and cold restart and over SW upgrade. Disabling during an active test aborts the ongoing OTDR test and allows the amplifier blocked by the automatic OTDR to be activated. Track it with auto-otdr-state: not-applicable, not-available, pass, in-progress, fail or aborted. Example: `set ots-r-auto-otdr-1-1-dwdm-line automatic-otdr enabled`.

Use `add oxcon-<name> source <value> destination <value>`, for example `add oxcon-1-80-192262500__1-3.1-dwdm-line-192262500 source 'nmc-1-80-192262500' destination 'nmc-1-3.1-dwdm-line-192262500'`. source and destination are the required instance-ID end-points and are add-only. Whether it comes up on its own is governed by activation-mode, also add-only: automatic activates the service automatically on creation and deactivates it on deletion, and is the default in standard L0 mode; manual (default for SLTE) and activate-on-create (default for HSC OLS) are driven by activation-request-fwd and activation-request-bwd, which take no-request, activate or deactivate. direction is two-way by default or one-way. Optional target-output-power-src and target-output-power-dst take -18.00..15.00 dBm, defaulting to 0 dBm or -5 dBm depending on the add/drop case.

Only the RD20TM. The `profile-control` command applies only to RD20TM operating in card-mode = slte or slte-backhaul, and its access mode is Operational Mode. Syntax is `profile-control [type=]<value> [entity=]<value> [direction=]<value> [[profile-data=]<value>]`. type is write-attenuation-profile, read-attenuation-profile, create-power-profile, read-power-profile or read-ocm-power. direction is tx or rx, but for power-profile only tx is supported. For RD20TM in card-mode = slte, the power profile and OCM power are defined at the output of the booster, before the EVOA, not at the DWDM line out port. OMS attenuation strings are <StartFreq>,<SlotWidth>,<AttnValue1>...<AttnValueN> with values 0 to 25.50 and N = 776 for standardC-band at 6.25 GHz; NMC values range -10 to 25.50 with N no greater than 32.

Not much. `set pump-<name>` exposes only three attributes: label, a user-defined string of length 0..256; admin-state, taking lock, unlock or maintenance; and alarm-report-control, allowed or inhibited, default Allowed. There is no power setting on this object. Everything else is read-only through `show pump-<name>`: supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, supported-facilities, AID, oper-state (enabled or disabled), avail-state (in-service, out-of-service, normal, abnormal, low-power), managed-by (system or user, and only user-created facilities can be user deleted) and pump-type. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. To set Raman pump power, use the separate `pump-power` command instead.

Use `set pump-power-<name>/<pump-id> target-pump-power <value>`, where pump-id is an integer identifying the number of the pump. target-pump-power is the Raman pump power required in dBm and applies when the control-mode is manual; the value range is -99.00..99.00 dBm or not-applicable, which is the default, and 0 is used for the not-applicable case. On an RPBM card the target-pump-power must be in the range 12 to 30 dBm. If the value is outside the operating range of the Raman sled, the alarm PUMP-Fail (STAT FAIL PSTAT) is raised. For the permitted limits read min-target-pump-power and max-target-pump-power, both decimal64 -99.00..99.00 dBm or not-applicable. configured-pump-power shows the power configured in hardware (derived automatically if control-mode is auto), and actual-pump-power the measured value, default -99.

Run `show raman-calibration-<name> calibration-state`, for example `show raman-calibration-1-8`. calibration-state displays the state of the automatic Raman gain calibration process: not-available (calibration has not been triggered or no prior calibration has occurred; the default), in-progress (currently running), up-to-date (completed successfully and up-to-date), out-dated (out-dated due to OTS OLOS, a change in delta pointloss and similar) or fail (ended with a failure). last-calibration-timestamp gives when the calibration RPC last completed with or without errors, or never. When the state is fail or out-dated, additional-info carries troubleshooting information (string 0..1024). Also readable: intermediate-results, gain-calibration-error, the residual gain error in dB after each iteration, and calibrated-delta-pointloss, -3..3.5 dB.

rsc is the Raman card Pilot Tone facility. `set rsc-<name>` accepts label, admin-state (Unlock, Locked, Maintenance, Unknown; default Unlocked) and alarm-report-control (Allowed or Inhibited, default Allowed). What it reports is pilot tone power: rsc-power-rx, the received Pilot Tone integrated power, and rsc-power-tx, the transmitted Pilot Tone integrated power, both carrying the value 99. `show rsc-<name>` additionally returns supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, supported-facilities, AID, oper-state (enabled or disabled, default enabled), avail-state and managed-by (system or user, default system, with only user-created facilities deletable by the user). Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Because the spectrum facility is only instantiated by the system when the underlying server layer, OMS, has monitoring-mode configured as either non-intrusive or ila-with-equalization. The existence of this managed object depends on the OMS monitoring-mode, and the object is only of relevance if the DGE2 is intended to be used in the NE. Set the OMS accordingly, for example `set oms-<name> monitoring-mode ila-with-equalization`, and the object appears. Once present, `set spectrum-<name>` takes label, admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control and attenuation-setting, a unique attenuation value for the entire spectrum, range 0..30 dB, default 0 dB, editable only if attenuation-control-mode = manual and control-mode = auto-max-pw. dge-in-use reports true when the corresponding OMS monitoring-mode is ila-with-equalization.

Use `spectrum-control`, keyed as <name>/<direction>/<center-frequency>, for example `set spectrum-control-1-7-dwdm-line2/egress/194943750 attenuation-target 1`. direction is ingress or egress, but only egress is currently supported (default egress), and center-frequency is the band slice center frequency in MHz, managed by the system. attenuation-target is the required attenuation for the spectra, range 0..30 dB, default 0, and is only possible to configure when a Dynamic Gain Equalizer or equivalent is in use, that is dge-in-use = true. target-output-power is the intended target output power for the spectra, not-specified (the default) or in the range -55..55 dBm. Read back attenuation-actual, readable only under the same DGE condition, and width, the detected width in MHz from spectrum-monitoring, returned as 0 if the frequency does not match or no ILAx card or DGE is fibre-connected.

Use the read-only spectrum-monitoring command: show spectrum-monitoring-<name>/<direction>/<center-frequency> [width] [lower-frequency] [upper-frequency] [target-actual-power] [power-actual] [psd-actual]. direction is ingress or egress, default egress, and only egress is currently supported; center-frequency is the band slice center frequency in MHz, managed by the system. width is the received NMC width in MHz, default 50000. power-actual is the currently received power in dBm, default -99, where -99 means the power has not yet been measured by the OCM at the DGE2 card or no power was detected; on egress it is calibrated at the DWDM line port output. target-actual-power (default -99dBm) is the ATPS-calculated target, relevant only when target-power-setting = auto. psd-actual is the calculated Power Spectral Density in nW/GHz to 2-digit precision, default not-applicable, and does not depend on spectral width. Example: show spectrum-monitoring-1-7-dwdm-line2/egress/191968750.

Read the contention-check-status attribute on the super-channel. It is settable on add (add super-channel-<name> carriers <value> carrier-mode <value> [label] [admin-state] [alarm-report-control] [contention-check-status]) and readable with show super-channel-<name> contention-check-status. Values are pending, success, overridden and failk, with pending as the default. The status is the Contention Check state set via DNA in openwave mode, and it is only applicable if openwave-contention-check is enabled at the super-channel-group level. openwave-contention-check enables the DNA-assisted contention control mechanism in openwave mode; its values are false and true, default false, and it is configured with add/set super-channel-group-<name> openwave-contention-check <value>. The related line-system-mode attribute defaults to openwave. Both commands run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

-m is the merge flag: Merge configuration, meaning the command will not fail if the entity already exists. The guide states the add command for super-channel-group works in merge mode only, so the -m flag performs a best-effort add: if the target entity does not exist it is created, and if it already exists it is updated with whatever attributes are present on the add command. Full syntax: add -m super-channel-group-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <lock|unlock|maintenance>] [auto-in-service-enabled <value>] [valid-signal-time <value>] [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>] [line-system-mode <value>] [openwave-contention-check <value>]. Defaults for those attributes are admin-state unlock, alarm-report-control allowed, auto-in-service-enabled false, line-system-mode openwave, and valid-signal-time 480 minutes (range 1..7200). The same -m merge flag is documented for comm-channel.

Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. carrier-mode is an acronymized handle of the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, string length 1...15, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, for example 600E.84P, 100X.73U or 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier in gbps, which is the per-mode capacity you are after. client-mode is the digital client mode mapped into and transported by the carriers in the superchannel, either ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate, application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for (string 1...15), compatibility-id identifies carrier modes applicable simultaneously, status is the state of the carrier mode, and supported-subtypes lists supported subtypes (string 0..32, maximum 20 elements).

Query the supported-gain-range object: show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. gain-range-type selects which of the three ranges you want and takes the values low, high or standard. gain-range-min returns the minimum settable gain-target for that type of range and gain-range-max returns the maximum settable gain-target, both of type gain-value; neither has a documented default (n/a), because the numbers are reported per instance rather than fixed by the guide. All parameters are used in show only; there is no set form. The name key is described in the parameter table as a flag to enable or disable access control, with values true/false and default false.

Different power profiles are supported to reflect different scenarios when using a card. The user can define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a given card type offers, use show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. card-type is the card type (string) and name is the profile name (string). profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0...255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, type decimal64. default is true or false and tells you whether that profile is the default one. All fields are show only; the command reports capability, it does not assign the profile.

The router ID comes from the router-id-mode attribute on the bgp-instance. router-id-mode takes use-loopback or manual and defaults to use-loopback, meaning the instance takes the loopback IP as its router ID unless you switch it to manual. When you need an explicit value, set the router-id attribute, which accepts an IPv6 or IPv4 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6, and it has no default. Syntax: add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], with set and delete forms available; instance-id is a string of length 1...255 and local-as is a number in the range 1..4294967295. The command runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example from the guide: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback.

On bgp-neighbor the three timers are connect-retry-interval, hold-time and keepalive-interval. connect-retry-interval is the seconds between attempts to establish a session with the peer, range 1..65535, default 120. hold-time is the seconds a session is considered active with no keepalive or other messages from the peer, range 3..65535, default 90, and is typically set to 3x the keepalive-interval. keepalive-interval is the seconds between keepalive transmissions, range 1..21845, default 30, typically 1/3 of the hold-time. The negotiated value is read back with negotiated-hold-time (0..65535, default 0). Yes, you can authenticate: secure-session sets the authentication method of the session to the peer and takes none or TCP-MD5, defaulting to none, with password supplying the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII, string 0..80. All are set via add/set bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address>.

The routes to be advertised to an external AS must already exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole, for example on add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> special-next-hop blackhole (the same parameter exists on ipv6-static-route). Beyond that, the bgp-network object itself just names what is exported: add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>, where instance-id is a string 1...255, remote-address is the peer in IPv4 or IPv6 form (0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported) and network-prefix is a decimal 1..64 or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured.

The mtu attribute of comm-channel is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when the mode is L3. The range is platform-dependent: 1280..1500 octets on the 1830 GX G30, and 1280..9202 octets on the 1830 GX G40. It is a uint16 integer. The default is 1500; on the 1830 GX G40 the per-interface-type defaults are 1518 for DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4. Set it with add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [mtu <value>] or set comm-channel-<name> mtu <value>, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The matching receive parameter, mru, is an integer in the range 64..1500 octets with default 1500 and is likewise only available in L3 mode.

LLDP is off by default: lldp-admin-status on comm-eth defaults to disabled, and its values are tx-only (transmits frames but does not store remote system information), rx-only (receives but does not transmit), tx-and-rx, and disabled. It cannot be modified if the mode is L1. Enable it with, for example, set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds, default 30. lldp-mgmt-addr-if picks which interface IP is advertised as the management address (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only), L0-MGMT); it must be set explicitly and applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled; rate (1/10/100/1000/10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum), duplex-mode (default full) and flow-control (default disabled) are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled.

Use the global dhcp-relay command: set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>], readable with show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]. It runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with disabled as the default, so relay is off until you pick an address family. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6, with no default; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples from the guide: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, and set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3. Per-interface activation is separate: if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled must also be set true on each interface, and it obeys these global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. Its values are manual, dhcp and both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts name servers from DHCP as well as ones you configure. Syntax: set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is the flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. search is the DNS-search-suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Per-server origin is tracked separately on dns-server, whose origin attribute is dhcp or manual with default manual.

Add a name server with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server; delete dns-server-<address> removes it and show dns-server-<address> [origin] displays it, all in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The origin attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where an entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the address has been manually configured.
