The default is manual. origin is also writable, so the user can convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one just by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. Example from the guide: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. The system-wide equivalent is the dns assignment-method attribute (manual, dhcp, both; default both).

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is per interface: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>] and show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. It is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on this interface; it takes true or false and defaults to false, and it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global set dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (not the default disabled) with a server-address configured for the interface setting to have effect. Examples from the guide: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true, and show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled. The interface object also lists an if-dhcp-relay attribute (false/true, default false) deciding on which interface the DHCP/v6 relay can run.

By default it is static and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> ..., ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive packets on each. protection-mode is the user-given protection mode, with values unknown (transient, output only), protected (protected by redundant ports) and unprotected (no port redundancy); it defaults to protected. The read-only protection-state reports the current protection with the same value set and defaults to unknown. Other defaults on add: admin-state unlock (lock, unlock, maintenance), alarm-report-control allowed, proxy-arp-enabled false (applicable only to the DCN interface). Note that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface.

Yes, that is exactly what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings a destination and its result takes action on configured static routes. Create one with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action taken when monitoring goes into failed state; its values are none and withdraw, and the default is withdraw. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the instance is not active until it is configured. probe-interval is 0...60 seconds, default 5; drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1; enabled defaults to true. The route side reports monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>. Read it back with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. The command runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and there is a pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. if-name is the interface object identifier, string length 0..64; type ? after ipv4-address- to list the available interfaces. Certain addresses are disallowed: those beginning with 0 (current network), those beginning with 127 (loopback), and those beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). netmask is the subnet expressed as a netmask and only valid netmasks are accepted. origin is show-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0.

distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. Syntax: add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. For a discard route, use special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole). Blackhole static routes exist because routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. advertised (true/false, default false) advertises the route in the routing protocol, as an AS external route for OSPF if OSPF is an ASBR; origin is manual or dhcp, default manual. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165.

It is the same shape but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported only on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. if-name is the interface object identifier, string length 0..64; type ? after ipv6-address- to see the object completion options. origin is show-only with values static, dhcp and auto-config, default static. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64.

Yes. The guide notes that static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and name DCN-B on the interface parameter, for example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B. The VRF bound to the interface must match the VRF provided on the static route. Defaults are distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), and special-next-hop blackhole for discard routes. The command is available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. The equivalent primary-interface form is add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. There may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to the LLDP neighbor and direction is ingress or egress. address is the string identifying the management address component of the remote system, length 0..64, whose purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype is unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the integer interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote agent, string 0..128.

They report the same kind of data from opposite ends, and differ in their key. management-address is keyed with a direction: show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>, where direction is ingress or egress. management-address-local drops that key: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>, and show management-address-local displays the management address information from the local LLDP ports. Both take the same optional fields if-subtype, if-id and address-oid, and both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. if-subtype is unknown (interface is not known), if-index (identifier based on the ifIndex MIB object) or system-port-number (identifier based on the system port numbering convention). address is a string 0..64 used to contact the management entity and address-oid is a string 0..128; on management-address-local the guide notes that address-oid is currently an empty string.

Yes, it is the use-as-source attribute of the networking object. Syntax: set networking [use-as-source <value>] and show networking [use-as-source], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. use-as-source is described as the interface to use as source address; its value is a string of length 0..64 and it has no default (n/a). You give it an interface name rather than a literal address. Example from the guide: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking displays the current setting. use-as-source is the only parameter the networking command defines.

show networking-services. That is the whole syntax: the command is used to show the list of network services, it takes no parameters, and it is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. There is no set form, only show. The guide's example is simply show networking-services. The related networking command is separate and carries the single use-as-source attribute (set networking use-as-source <interface>).

Because the RIB is the organising container: each next-hop entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family, and for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. So the next-hop AID is keyed by RIB first: show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]. rib-name is a String of length 1..64 matching pattern '([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*)', destination-prefix is an IP prefix, interface is the outgoing interface reference (for example DCN), and next-hop-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN, or plain show next-hop for all entries.

Use clear ospf. Syntax: clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>. It removes and restarts an ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the CLI does not wait for the restart to complete. The instance parameter is the id of the ospf-instance, given as a string, and there is no default. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation; without it you are prompted to confirm. Access mode is Operational Mode only. Example: clear ospf 1. Note that ospf-instance itself is added, set, shown and deleted with the ospf-instance commands; clear ospf is the asynchronous restart path referenced from that section.

No. The ospf-area commands accept only one area type: ospf-area-type has the single permitted value normal, and normal is also the default. Stub and NSSA are not offered. Syntax: add|set ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>], show ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type], delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>. instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0.

Use ospf-area-range, which summarises routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask and is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only. Syntax: add|set ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>], show ... [advertise], delete ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix>. advertise takes true or false (advertise or hide) and defaults to true. prefix is an IPv4 prefix with length <= 32 or an IPv6 prefix with length <= 128, in canonical form with non-prefix bits zero. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true.

Yes. ospf-instance has a version attribute taking ospfv2 or ospfv3, with ospfv2 as the default, settable only at add time. Syntax: add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]. instance-id is uint8 0..255, router-id is a dotted-quad, description is a String of length 0..128. The router id is chosen by router-id-mode, which takes manual or use-loopback and defaults to use-loopback. Pre-condition: if router-id-mode is use-loopback then an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. show also exposes vrf. Example: add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3.

On ospf-interface the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Related timers: retransmission-interval default 5 seconds (2..3600) and transmit-delay default 1 second (1..450). Also ospf-cost default 10 (1..65535) and priority default 1 (0..255, where 0 means not eligible for DR/BDR). Authentication is available: ospf-auth-enable takes true or false and defaults to false; ospf-auth-algorithm takes none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256; ospf-auth-key is an ASCII string of length 0..256. The algorithm and key are only of relevance for ospfv2. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must be present.

Use show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority], in Operational Mode. The state values are: down (initial, no Hello packets received), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor packets with LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs), and full (full adjacency achieved). The role values are drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Note: an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Use ospfv3-ipsec-security-association. Syntax: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>], plus set, show and delete on the same AID. spi is a unique security parameter index, uint32 in range 256..4294967295. integrity-algorithm is mandatory on add and takes AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 or AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96. ipsec-protocol supports ESP only (default ESP) and ipsec-mode supports transport only (default transport). Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128.

Use ping with -i or -v: ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -c=<count> stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, -w=<timeout> sets a timeout in seconds before ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and -s=<pktsize> sets the octets sent exclusive of headers, default 56 plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total packet size of 64 octets. ping-dest may be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show protocols, which lists all of them in one place: ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig. Syntax: show protocols [ssh|cli|serial-console|netconf|grpc|snmp|restconf|http-file-server|data-model-openconfig]; naming one drills into its settings. Sample output shows ssh with enabled false on port 8022 plus host keys and pre/post-login messages; cli enabled true on port 22 with script-dir '/storage/scripts'; serial-console with global-switch enabled and global-timeout 60 minutes; netconf enabled true on port 830; restconf enabled true, https-enabled true, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout 5 minutes, api-root '/restconf'; grpc enabled true on port 50051; snmp enabled true on port 161; http-file-server https-port 8981 with url-base '/transfer'. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family, and for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB for each supported address family. rib-name is a String of length 1..64. address-family takes ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast. vrf is the VRF to which this RIB is bound, a leafref on path "../../vrf/name". There are no defaults on these parameters. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show rib-IPv4 views the RIB identified by the 'IPv4' key.

Use show route, which lists system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static route. Syntax: show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]. The source-protocol attribute gives the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP, static. rib-name is a String of length 1..64 and destination-prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. special-next-hop shows special treatment applied to IPv4/IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring: none (no special treatment, used for all normal routes), blackhole (no next-hop is created under the route) or unreachable (no next-hop is created under the route); the default is none. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show route.

Yes: show routing. It is used to show routing information, takes no parameters at all, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show routing. From there the detail is in the neighbouring show commands: show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family] for the per-address-family RIBs, show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol] for the route list with its source protocol, show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> for next-hop detail, show vrf-<name> for the routing instances, and show protocols for the management protocol set.

show supporting-interface reports supporting interface information, that is which underlying IPv4/IPv6 interface backs a given interface. Syntax: show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface>. The name parameter is the name of the interface, a string. The interface parameter is a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface, expressed as a path, and its value is ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name, so it resolves to an if-name under networking/interface. Both parameters are used in show only; neither has a default. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

The default maximum is 30 hops and the default VRF is MGMT. Syntax: traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]. -m=<hopcnt> is the maximum number of hops (max time-to-live), uint8 range 1..255, default 30. -w=<timeout> is the timeout in seconds, uint16 range 1..10, default 2. -v=<vrf> is a string and defaults to MGMT; -i=<interface> selects the source interface and by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. pktsize is the total probe packet size, uint16, default 60 (60 bytes for IPv4). tr-dest may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain-name. Example: traceroute -m=10 -w=3 1.2.3.4.

Use show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description]. The chassis-name attribute gives the associated chassis name for that VRF. name is a String of length 0..32, type is either mgmt (Management VRF) or internal (Internal VRF), and description is a String of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose. None of these have defaults. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show vrf-MGMT views the Management VRF attributes. Plain show vrf lists the instances. The vrf name is also referenced from rib (vrf leafref "../../vrf/name") and from ospf-instance.

Yes, a successful swimage activation implies a system restart. Syntax: activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>], in Operational Mode. db-action specifies the expected database operation: auto activates the image processing the database with the system default behavior, empty-db activates with an empty database, upgrade-db activates by upgrading the current database, and rollback rolls back to the previous active software image. The default is auto, so if you do not provide it the system decides automatically. Unless -f is given the user must confirm the activation when prompted; -v forces the validate check again. label specifies the sw image/manifest file name; if not specified the currently installable image is used. Example: activate swimage db-action=empty-db.

No: only a single location led test can be running at a time, and not all cards support the Location LED test functionality. Syntax: activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>], Operational Mode. entity is a chassis or a card, for example activate location-led card-1-1. led-mode is flash (default, amber light blinking at 1Hz, used for LED location) or solid (steady amber, used for lamp test, which lights all chassis LEDs amber). To turn it off use terminate location-led [entity=]<value>, or set timeout, a number in range 0..120 seconds, default 0 meaning no timeout so the function runs until terminated. Note the timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, so use terminate there.

Use bootstrap, which establishes a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisions the initial administrator account on a neighbor NE that has no configured users yet. Syntax: bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>. Select the neighbour either by local-port, the supporting-port of a MGMT vrf osc-eth interface as shown by show interface (for example 1-1-dwdm-line1), which the system maps to the OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id> netdev and resolves to the peer address with get_osc_neighbors.sh (if resolution fails the RPC is rejected), or by neighbor-address directly, the IPv6 link-local address including zone, string length 7..256, pattern 'fe80:.*'. new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32. new-password may be a $6$ SHA512 hash or plain text. Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Type cancel-upgrade. Syntax: cancel-upgrade [-h]. It cancels any active upgrade in progress. The only flag is -h, which displays help for this command. Pre-condition: an upgrade must be in progress for this command to execute successfully. Access mode is Operational mode. Example: cancel-upgrade.

change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so on an in-service node you lose the configuration. Syntax: change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value>, where ztp-mode is enabled or disabled and has no default. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, so without it you are prompted first. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and will stop ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. The current ztp mode configuration is displayed with show ztp. Access mode is Operational mode. Example: change-ztp-mode disabled.

Use show current-fw and read the fw-status attribute against fw-version and expected-fw-version. Syntax: show current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name> [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status], with the same form for <card-name>.<slot-name>, <chassis-name>-<slot-name> and <name>. fw-status takes current (current firmware is up-to-date), not-current (current firmware is not up-to-date against the expected one) or unavailable (information on firmware status is currently unavailable); the default is unavailable. fw-name, fw-version and expected-fw-version are Strings of length 0..32. Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example output: current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT fw-version 0x20, expected-fw-version 0x28, fw-status not-current.

The download filetype values are crl (a CRL file in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 X.509 end-entity cert), peer-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#12), script (a CLI script), swimage (a manifest file then all files belonging to a SW image), and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place; there is no need to provide a local storage location. The exception is filetype file, where the destination parameter may be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name only, a relative path or an absolute path, and you need write access to it. Use show transfer to see the default storage directory. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp.

Use show downloaded-image, which retrieves information about downloaded image files. Syntax: show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]. The signature attribute is the downloaded software image file signature, a String of length 0..1024. manifest-file is the downloaded manifest file and its information, a String of length 0..256, and name is the name of the downloaded software image, also a String of length 0..256. All three are used in show only and have no defaults. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show downloaded-image lists all downloaded software image files.

show downloads. Syntax is exactly show downloads, with no parameters. It shows a list of downloads. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands for the same area: show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature] for downloaded software image files and their signature, show transfer-status for the progress of an asynchronous download started with download -a, and show transfer for the default storage directory.

Yes, within limits. The file command (Operational mode) performs basic file and directory operations: rename, view (listing for a file or directory), delete, sha256sum and md5sum. Its parameters are operation, file-path, new-file-path (used only when operation is rename) and result. File system access is restricted to the current user's access, so not all files and directories are editable. Examples: file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log, file view /tmp, file delete /tmp/a.log, file sha256sum /tmp/a.log. Separately, clear [-f] file filetype target-file removes one particular file; filetype is limited to krp (only one KRP may exist, so target-file is not needed), script (use show script to list them) and swimage (deletes a downloaded swimage that was not yet installed). show file <filename> displays the file contents.

Both are described as performing basic file and directory operations and both run in Operational mode, but file is the fuller command. file-operation takes only operation (rename, delete, view), new-file-path and file-path. file takes operation with five values (rename, delete, view, sha256sum, md5sum), plus file-path, new-file-path (for rename) and a result attribute reporting the file operation result, and it carries the companion forms show file <filename> to display file contents and clear [-f] file <filetype> <target-file> to remove a krp, script or downloaded swimage. So use file for checksums, viewing contents and clearing typed files; file-operation covers only rename/delete/view.

Use add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port] [user-name] [password] [initial-path] [label], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; set, show file-server-<name>, show file-servers and delete file-server-<name> also exist. The protocol values are file, ftp, sftp, scp, http and https. file represents local storage, including USB storage, and requires initial-path to be provided. ftp and http are only applicable when secure-mode is set to false. server-address may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain name. server-port is optional: if not provided the default for the selected protocol is used. Limits: name 0-64 characters, user-name 0-64, password 0-128, initial-path 0-256, label 0-256.

Use show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is the file type for which the transfer happened. last-transfer is the last transfer start timestamp, a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see the set-time command). last-duration is the last transfer duration as a time-interval, last-completion-status is the last transfer status, and last-operation is the last transfer operation with values unknown, upload or download. Note that transfer status only exists if at least one operation of that kind was done for the specified filetype.

Yes, but it is off by default. set http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] and show http-file-server (which also shows url-base) run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is the master switch to enable or disable file server access and defaults to true. http-enabled enables plain HTTP and defaults to false; https-enabled defaults to true. The default http-port is 8980 and the default https-port is 8981; both are user configurable numbers. url-base is the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application, a string of 1 to 100 characters with the value /transfer.

Use the manifest commands in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information] gives the manifest itself: manifest-signature is a hex-string up to 1024, downloaded-on is the download timestamp in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format, and information is a string up to 256. show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description] gives each package: state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version is up to 64 characters and description up to 512. show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version] gives the firmware carried per equipment-type.

No. The packaged-fw command shows the firmware version included in a software-load, and versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type. Use show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version] or show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; show packaged-fw lists them all. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> (string 0-64). swload-state is active, inactive or installable. equipment-type is the card or other equipment type that will use the firmware (0-32 characters), fw-name is the firmware name (0-32) and fw-version the included version (0-32).

Yes. prepare-upgrade has two options: validate, which validates the software label or manifest, and apply, which applies it. Syntax: prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] option=<value> manifest=<value> [db-action=<value>] [clear-type=<value>] script=<value> new-admin-user=<value> new-admin-password=<value>, in Operational mode. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after prepare-upgrade apply), -f force without confirmation. Example: prepare-upgrade validate <label>, then prepare-upgrade apply <label>. db-action (unattended only) is empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, default upgrade-db. clear-type is full (default), keep-networking or initialize-from-script, and is only valid for an unattended operation with db-action empty-db.

clear recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag. It clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. As such, it may be traffic impacting. The command has no parameters. Syntax: clear [-f] recover-mode, in Operational mode. The only flag is -f, which forces the command without the confirmation prompt: clear -f recover-mode.

Use show software-load-<swload-state> or show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. swload-state is active (active software load), inactive (inactive software load) or installable (installable software load). Attributes are swload-version, swload-manifest and swload-prepared (true/false, both only relevant for the installable load), swload-status, swload-information, swload-activation-type, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. swload-activation-type applies only to state installable and is direct (no reboot type determined), warmstart (warm reboot required) or coldstart (cold reboot required). Examples: show software-load-active, show software-load-1-5/active.

Use show software-location-<location-id>, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. location-id is the location of the equipment, a string of up to 64 characters, expressed as <chassis-id>-<slot-id>. For example, show software-location-1-5 retrieves software location information from the card in chassis 1, slot 5. To narrow it to a particular load state on that slot, use show sw-management software-location-<shelf>-<slot> software-load-active (or software-load-inactive or software-load-installable), for example show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active, which returns the software-load-1-4/active entry with its sw-component list, swload-version, swload-vendor, swload-product and swload-label.

Use show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. card-type and subtype each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which the constraints apply, strings of 1 to 20 characters. min-capacity is the minimum capacity supported by the subtype in gbps and max-capacity the maximum in gbps, where -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. supported-applications lists the applications supported by the subtype and unsupported-applications those not supported; if either list is empty, that constraint is not applicable. description is a string of 1 to 255 characters.

Use show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description], or show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name> when not scoping to a slot; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The state attribute is the package state: installed (software package installed), not-installed (not installed), installation-failed (install failed) or unknown (state unknown), with unknown as the default, so installation-failed is what you look for. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state is active, inactive or installable. version is up to 64 characters and description up to 512. Examples: show sw-component, show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg.

Use show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime], which lists the OS-level containers; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. cpu-usage is the current CPU usage by the container as a percentage in the range 0 to 100, and in a multi-core system it indicates the overall usage relative to all cores. memory-usage is the current memory usage as a percentage, range 0 to 100. state is off (default state, the container is not launched yet), up (running) or exited. equipment is a reference to the card AID on which the container runs, and uptime is the time since the container started. Examples: show sw-container, show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi.

Yes. sw-control-rule adds service-specific custom rules that override the default action upon service failure. Syntax: add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>, set sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action <value>], show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action], delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. service-name is the name of the service to be monitored, a string up to 64 characters. fail-action values are default-action (restart the service, then reboot the system if the service does not recover), ignore (no automatic action on service failure) and system-restart (warm restart the system or card software immediately on failure). Example: add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action.

Yes. show sw-management gives software locations, activity and downloads in one place, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: show sw-management [downloads | software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active | software-load-inactive | software-load-installable] | software-load-active | software-load-inactive]. show sw-management downloads lists the download history, for example the downloaded manifest files. show sw-management software-load-active lists the active load's sw-component and packaged-fw entries plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label; software-load-inactive does the same for the inactive load. show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active scopes it to one shelf and slot.

Use show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count], or show sw-services for all of them; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. reboot-count is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16. Pair it with last-start-time, the time of the last service start or boot, a date-time in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format, and uptime, the time since the service turned up in days:hours:minutes. state is off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch or unresponsive), with state-details giving a brief description. Example: show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr.

sw-subcomponent drills one level below sw-component: it keys on the subcomponent inside a package rather than the package itself. Syntax: show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description], or show sw-subcomponent-<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. sw-component-name and sw-subcomponent-name are strings of 1 to 256 characters. The reported attributes are the same set as sw-component: state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown, default unknown), version (0-64) and description (0-512). Example: show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb, versus show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg.

Run swversion. It retrieves the active, inactive and installable versions of the software present on the network element, takes no parameters, and works in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The output lists software-load-active, software-load-inactive and software-load-installable at NE level with the version and label, and then the same three states per location, for example software-load-1-1/active, software-load-1-1/inactive and software-load-1-1/installable. A sample line reads: software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188. For more detail on any one entry use show software-load-<state> or show sw-management.

Use show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. file-status is the firmware file status with values valid, invalid or missing. crc is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present, up to 64 characters. applicable-eqpt is the list of resources that this firmware can be applied to and present-in-eqpt the list of resources that contain this version, each with max-elements 80. path (up to 255), version, vendor and part-number (each up to 64) identify the image, and nsa-upgrade-version lists the versions from which the upgrade is non service affecting.

Set it with set transfer http-proxy <value> and read it back with show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. http-proxy is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, that is CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Note that this proxy is not used for file transfers. The value is a string up to 1024 characters in the format [http://]<host>[:<port>], where http:// is optional, host may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and port is optional; if port is omitted the default is 1080. Example: set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080.

Use show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details], or plain show transfer-status for all entries. operation is upload or download. transfer-progress is the completion percentage, 0-100, default 0; bytes-transferred is the bytes transferred so far and total-bytes the total file size, both uint64 defaulting to 0, with total-bytes zero until known at transfer start. details gives the transfer phase: completed, Failed, idle, preparation or transfer, default idle. last-completion-status may be success, fail, in-progress or unknown, where unknown occurs if the system rebooted mid-transfer. transfer-type is sync or async.

Use show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. resource may represent the entire ne, a chassis or a card; for ne and chassis the results are aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope, so start at ne and drill down to find the failing card. status values include idle, upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-partially-failed, upgrade-failed, validate-in-progress/failed/complete, apply-in-progress/failed/complete, activate-in-progress/failed/complete, cancel-in-progress/complete/failed and no-communication; default idle. step is the identifier of the current upgrade step and step-start-time when it began; start-time and end-time show na if the entity was idle or has not finished a phase since startup. details carries up to 255 characters of explanation.

Use upload [-a] [-s] filetype=debug-log with either destination=<URL> or file-server=<name> [path=<value>]; debug-log uploads logs for diagnostic troubleshooting and includes all other logs. debug-entity is mandatory for debug-log and restricts collection to a particular card or chassis; if absent all data is included. optional-content adds optional content to debug-logs. -a runs the upload asynchronously (check it with show transfer-status); in synchronous mode a textual progress bar is rendered live. -s skips TLS verification for HTTPS and ssh known host checking for SCP/SFTP. Certificates differ: for local-certificate, peer-certificate and trusted-certificate you must give certificate-name, except for trusted-certificate where omitting it exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not, and output files are in P7 pem format.

Use show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. ztp-state is the current state of the ZTP service, with values ztp-init (the default), dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress, ztp-completed, ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart. ztp-details adds information on the current state, up to 256 characters. ztp-completion-status summarizes ZTP on the node as not-completed (default) or completed. ztp-mode is the user-set mode, disabled or enabled with enabled as the default, and is set via the change-ztp-mode RPC, which is allowed even when the NBI is locked.

Use the capabilities command: 'show capabilities-<name>', where 'name' is the name of the card (string, no default). It retrieves the information about that card's capabilities. The command is available in Operational mode and in Candidate Configuration mode. It is a show-only object: there is no add, set or delete form. For capability data indexed by card type rather than by an installed card instance, the related objects are supported-card (per card-type), supported-port (per card-type/port-name), supported-slot and supported-tom.

To provision a card you use 'add card-<name>' and must supply three mandatory attributes: required-type (the card type, String length 0..32, for example CHM1R, CHM6, CHM7, XMM4, UTM2, FAN, PEM, BLANK), chassis-name (String length 1...255, default 1) and slot-name (String). Optional attributes on add are required-subtype, card-mode, subslot-name, power-profile, alias-name, admin-state (lock/maintenance/unlock, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default Inhibited) and label. subslot-name can only be set at (sub)card creation. Example: add card-1-4 required-type CHM1R chassis-name 1 slot-name 2.

On 1830 GX G40 you must set the chassis ambient temperature to 40C before a Native ZR TOM will come up. If configured-ambient-temperature is not set, the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. The attribute is configured-ambient-temperature on the chassis object, a number in Celsius units, settable with 'add chassis-<name>' or 'set chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature <value>' and readable with 'show chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature'. It has no default. It is the value used to compute the FRU's power consumption.

The console object carries baud-rate, set with 'set console-<name> baud-rate <value>' and read with 'show console-<name> [baud-rate] [actual-baud-rate] [auto-sensing-state] [local-switch] [status]'. Permitted values are auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200. The default is 9600 on 1830 GX G30 and 115200 on 1830 GX G40. Yes, it can work it out itself: with auto-sensing the system detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client, then locks it; the detected rate appears in actual-baud-rate and auto-sensing-state shows sensing or locked (default sensing). Not all cards support auto-sensing; check console-port-support and default-console-baud-rate on supported-card.

Use 'show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]'. redundancy-status is active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). redundancy-standby-status tells you readiness: ready-synchronized means the standby controller is in sync and ready; other values are not-ready-synchronizing (default), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out (protection in lock-out) and card-not-present. number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are only visible on the active controller card. additional-details is a string (0..128) with extra synchronization detail.

Use 'show equipment [<option>]', available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. With no option it displays all installed equipment; the available options vary according to your installation. To restrict output to one card, give the card object as the option, for example 'show equipment card-1-1'. The per-card output lists the child objects (controller-card-1-1, console-1-1, port-1-1-AUX-1, port-1-1-CRAFT, port-1-1-DCN, port-1-1-U1) and the card attributes: required-type, required-subtype, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control and label.

Both are controlled by equipment-policies: 'set equipment-policies [tom-auto-migration <value>] [auto-assigned-directions <value>] [auto-assigned-degrees <value>] [cable-id-control <value>] [chassis-assignment-mode <value>] [comm-eth-location <value>]'. tom-auto-migration (enabled/disabled) enables automatic update of the TOM subtype based on the present equipment; it may directly impact existing configurations and it covers subtype migration only, not TOM type migration (no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28). auto-assigned-degrees (enabled/disabled) is disabled by default, but enabled if l0-mode-op is hsc-ols, so degrees are not assigned automatically unless you enable it. auto-assigned-directions is enabled by default.

You have to enable it. 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <value>' turns SerDes templates on globally; values are enabled and disabled, default disabled (the CLI value completion offers false and true). On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively: they are applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact, and the existing SerDes configuration is kept on all TOMs whether it came from a template or was set manually. Read it back with 'show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates'. Application of any serdes-template depends on this flag being true; use apply-template to force re-application.

Use 'show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>'. It displays the packaged FRU information associated with a particular equipment-type. manifest-file is the manifest file, a string of length 0..256; equipment-type is the type of the equipment, a string of length 0..32. Neither has a default. The command is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode and is show-only. For the data of a physically present FRU (serial number, CLEI, part number, hardware version) use the inventory command instead.

Use the inventory command, which shows data for a present FRU: 'show inventory-<name>', 'show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>', 'show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>' or 'show inventory-<card-name>.<slot-name>'. Request serial-number (Serial number of the equipment) and clei (Common Language Equipment Identifier), both strings. Other attributes available on the same object are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision (default 0), PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ or 'NA'), number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class, actual-max-power-draw and fw-status. Example: show inventory-1-3-1.

Use 'show led-<location>/<name> [status]' or 'show leds'. location is the AID of the equipment location of the LED (chassis, card or port AID, string 1..32) and name is the LED name within the FRU (string 1..16). The object exists even if the FRU is not physically present; in that case status reads not-available, which is also the default. The status values are: not-available, off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off (cycles all supported colors including off), cycling (cycles all colors excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber. Example LEDs: led-1-1/active, led-1-1/fault, led-1-PEM-1/status.

In 1830 GX G40 there are three physical categories: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports exist on XMMs only and are found on Slot 1 XMMs. The trib/line ports appear on a CHM6 or CHM7 (slots 4-7) only after a TOM is provisioned in that CHM6/CHM7. Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. The port-type attribute, shown with 'show port-<card-name>-<port-name> port-type', enumerates: line (colored CWDM/DWDM line-side module), tributary (grey client interfaces), tributary-subport (a tributary split into subports), usb, comm, uplink (aggregation ports to an adjunct line function), optical, otdr, ocm and pluggable (the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM).

Use 'show resources-<name> [internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth] [internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth] [paired-slot-total-bandwidth] [paired-slot-available-bandwidth]'. These four bandwidth attributes apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards; the paired-slot pair applies only to SPN2/SPN2C cards that support Paired Slots. Internal cell-switch total and available bandwidth default to 600.000 Gbit/s when the card has paired slot interconnection capability. Paired-slot total and available bandwidth default to 500.000 Gbit/s with that capability and to 0 without it. The same object also shows supported-carriers, unassigned-carriers and supported-sub-components. Example: show resources-254-1.

Read the status leaf on the serdes object: 'show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> [value] [status]'. status is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once it is configured, with values set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown, the default), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported). A bare 'show serdes' lists every parameter with its value and status, for example serdes-1-7-T1/TxEQ 1 set. The parameter itself is created with 'add serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value>', changed with set, and removed with delete.

A serdes-template is keyed by TOM part number and is created per tom-part-number: 'add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]'. tom-part-number is a string of length 1..16. Templates apply to all line cards that support serdes; when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in the template is applied automatically. You can narrow the ports with ports-applicable, whose values are 'all' (the default behavior: all ports considered) or port names, string length 1..16, maximum 20 elements. Manual serdes configuration is still allowed and kept even when it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists. Application depends on use-serdes-templates being true; force re-application with apply-template.

Each individual parameter is a serdes-template-entry, composed of a serdes parameter name and its value: 'add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>'. Edit with 'set serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> [value <value>]', remove with delete, and display with 'show serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name>/<name> [value]'. name is the name of the serdes parameter, string length 0..256; value is the value of the serdes parameter, string length 0..256; tom-part-number identifies the template, string length 1..16. Example: add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3.

Yes. The serial-console object holds the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system and is managed by the system, so it cannot be manually deleted. Use 'set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]' and 'show serial-console [global-switch] [global-timeout]'. global-switch allows access by serial console, values enabled and disabled, default enabled; each console port can override this global behavior via the console object's local-switch (use-global-switch, force-enable, force-disable). global-timeout is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes, default 60, and can be set to zero to disable the inactivity timer. Example: set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80.

Use the slot equipment holder object: 'show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> [AID] [supported-type] [installed-type] [oper-state] [avail-state] [current-equipment]', or 'show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>' for a subslot. current-equipment names the equipment currently required in this slot (for example 1-1). installed-type is what is physically there and supported-type lists what the slot accepts, for example CHM6,gx:UCM4 on slots 5-7 of a G42. oper-state is enabled or disabled (default disabled) and avail-state reports values such as normal in-service or partially-faulted abnormal in-service. A bare 'show slot' lists every slot in the node. For what could go there by card type, see supported-slot possible-card-types.

Use 'show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]', available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. card-name is the card supporting the sub-component (string 0..64 characters), sub-component-name is the sub-component name, AID is the Resource Access Identifier (string 1..64) and description is a user configurable description (string 0..128). A bare 'show sub-component' lists them all, for example sub-component-1-6/dco-oec with AID 1-6-dco-oec, described as the DCO OEC (Optical Engine Controller) sub-component, and sub-component-1-6/dco-secproc, the DCO Security Processor. You can also see the names of a card's sub-components via 'show resources-<name> supported-sub-components', which lists those addressable for operations like restart.

Use 'show supported-card-<card-type> node-type-compatibility'. node-type-compatibility gives the supported NE node-type for a sled card and is only of relevance for line-cards and carrier-cards. The values are all (compatible with any node-type), ILA (In-Line Amplifier, two-directions) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer). So the card is usable on an in-line amplifier node if the value is ILA or all. The same command exposes sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. Example: show supported-card-CHM1R.

Use 'show supported-chassis-<chassis-type>', where chassis-type is an identityref such as G31, G32, G34c or G42. controller-redundancy-supported is true or false and states whether that chassis supports controller redundancy. Slot counts come from number-of-front-slots and number-of-rear-slots, both uint8. For example supported-chassis-G42 reports controller-redundancy-supported true, power-control-supported true, depth 600 mm, height 3 RUs, 7 front slots and 12 rear slots. Other attributes are supported-subtype, default-subtype, description, fan-adjustment-on-altitude (default false), dust-filter-replacement (not-applicable, optional-dust-filter default, dust-filter-regularly-replaced), leds, supported-subchassis-type (max 10 elements; empty means no multi-chassis) and supported-features.

Use 'show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>', for example 'show supported-port-CHM1R/2'. port-type says what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, ocm or pluggable (the L0 cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM). configuration-mode says who configures it: system-configured means the system configures it automatically and the user cannot make changes, user-configured means you can provision or de-provision. The object also exposes direction (not-applicable, tx, rx, rxtx), faceplate-label (1..36), leds (max 10), present (always, or in-node-controller-only), default-tom (default none), parent-port, subport-list, and allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true) which says whether TOMs on this port type follow the equipment-policies tom-auto-migration flag.

Use 'show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name>' (or supported-slot-<card-type>/<slot-name> for subslots). requires-blank-when-empty answers the blank question with not-applicable, optional or required. On a G42, slots 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and PEM-1 through PEM-4 are 'required'; slot 2, the FAN slots and FANCTRL-1 are 'not-applicable'. possible-card-types lists which cards can go in the slot, maximum 15 elements, for example XMM4 for slot 1, IOPANEL for slot 2 and CHM6,UCM4 for slots 4-7. The same command shows slot-location (front/rear), slot-vertical-position, slot-horizontal-position, configuration-mode (system-configured or user-configured), auto-provision-capable, default-card, reset-power in W at 55 degrees C, virtual-slot (default false) and leds (max 10).

Use 'show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> [supported-subtype] [supported-phy-modes] [default-phy-mode]'. tom-type is the form factor, for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28 or QSFPDD; tom-subtype-group is a string of length 0..32, for example '4x100GE-breakout'. supported-phy-mode gives the phy-modes supported by that TOM on that card and default-phy-mode gives the one used by default; both take values from 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G and 200G. supported-subtype lists the subtypes allowed for that TOM type in that card/port. Examples: show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28 and show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout.

Use 'show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> [supported-power-class] [supported-max-power-draw]', where tom-type is the pluggable form factor identity matching the TOM required-type (for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28, QSFPDD). supported-power-class is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, uint8 in the range 1..8; the port may only partially support that class, so read supported-max-power-draw, a decimal64 giving the maximum power in watts the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class. What the fitted module actually reports is on the inventory object as actual-power-class (uint8, 1..8) and actual-max-power-draw, populated only for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules.

Yes. When you create a TOM with add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>, the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. required-type is mandatory on add and takes CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Optional attributes on add/set are required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (false/true, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; CHM7 cards only). Example: add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD. Access mode is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show tom-type-<tom-type> support-third-party-toms. That attribute is a boolean (false, true) that states whether the TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to the supported Nokia TOMs. The same command also returns description (string 0..255), data-rate (uint16, in Gbps), and generic-subtype, which is the 3rd party subtype for that TOM. Run show tom-type on its own to list all supported TOM types. tom-type is read-only (show only) and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the TOM itself, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) exists specifically to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It appears under unprovisioned-inventory, which lists equipment detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration. Use show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>. The chassis-serial-number is the residing chassis serial number (string 0..16) and slot-name is the residing slot (string 0..16); if the equipment is the chassis itself, slot-name is empty. Readable attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format, see set-time), and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected the unprovisioned equipment. Available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path], for example show usb-1-5-U1. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted and can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations. available-space is the current free space and total-space is the total space, both uint16 in MB. All three attributes apply only when type is storage; the other type value is power-supply, which is for powering external equipment such as passive shelves. present (true/false, default false) shows whether the connector is inserted. Run show usb with no AID to list every USB port on the node with its type and present state. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>] from Operational mode. The pre-condition is that a snapshot must already have been taken (see take-snapshot) before it can be activated. db-instance names the snapshot to activate and defaults to temp; paraphrase is a short description of the database being activated and must be 40 to 200 characters. sanity-check-override takes true or false and defaults to false, so the sanity check runs unless you explicitly override it. Examples from the guide: activate-snapshot onehour activates the snapshot named onehour, and activate-snapshot sanity-check-override activates with the sanity check overridden.

Advanced parameter commands only take effect on the node after enable-advanced-parameters on the optical carrier is set to true. That is the prerequisite for add, set, show and delete of advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name>. Two documented behaviours explain what you are seeing: if no advanced parameter is configured, or it has been deleted, show advanced-parameter reports ERROR: object does not exist; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected, but show advanced-parameter reports status failed. The status attribute values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown, with unknown as the default. Supported parameter names and values for CHM6 and CHM7/7X are in the 1830 GX System Description Guide.

Use apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*]). Set template-type to serdes-template (the default value shown is serdes-templage), which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOMs given in applicable-tom. If applicable-tom is not provided, or the list is empty, all system TOMs are considered for template application. Example: apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1. This is the way to force re-application of a serdes-template to already-installed pluggables. Note that template application depends on the global flag use-serdes-templates being enabled (set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates, default disabled); enabling it does not retroactively apply templates, they are applied from that moment onward. Access: Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>] from Candidate Configuration mode (entered with configure). The candidate is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not arrive before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a persist trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. Confirm with commit persist and abandon with commit cancel. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit the commands require the -id parameter, and that same <id> is used on commit confirmed, commit persist and the confirmed cancel. Plain commit commits without a timer, and commit -m=<message> attaches a custom message.

Run show config and pipe it through the display filter: show config | display commands, then store the result for later use. The guide gives this exactly as the good way to create a CLI script that can restore the system configuration. show config displays the system configuration with non-default values only (anything left at its default is skipped), and the output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. You can narrow it with show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]: supply an entity-id to limit output to one instance, or an entity-type if all entities of that type are relevant. The saved script can then be replayed, for example via configure from-script=<script>.

It depends on the target you choose. configure <target> takes exclusive or shared, and exclusive is the default. In exclusive mode only your session can make changes to the candidate configuration; in shared mode multiple sessions can change the candidate configuration concurrently. The command moves you from Operational mode into Candidate Configuration mode and is only issued from Operational mode. You can also control where the candidate starts from: by default it starts as a copy of the Running Datastore; from-default starts from a blank config, removing all non-default configuration from the candidate; from-script=<script> imports a CLI command text file, replacing the running configuration with the script contents; and from-commit=<commit-id> initialises from a past commit-record, which is only available when commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: configure exclusive.

Use show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]. This command shows the current values of the advanced parameters that are actually running on the system, which can differ from what you configured with advanced-parameter. Run show current-advanced-parameter with no AID for everything, or scope it to one carrier, for example show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*. Parameters are optical-carrier-name (string), current-advanced-parameter-name (string) and value (string, the value running on the system). Output lines look like current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/EEPNNLMitigation 0 1. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Note that PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified; it is to be supported in a future release.

No. clear database sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, and it is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity, but it does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data. Use the clear system command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. Syntax: clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>, with -f forcing it without confirmation. clear-type is full (default; reset to factory defaults), keep-networking (full wipe but network configuration retained), or initialize-from-script (full wipe then initialise from a pre-stored .cli script, absolute path or filename under /storage/scripts). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Expect transient alarms after the controller reboot; they can be ignored.

Use db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value> from Operational Mode, with type set to encryption-with-integrity. The two permitted type values are encryption and encryption-with-integrity; encryption-with-integrity is the mode that adds an integrity check on top of database encryption. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The migration automatically reboots the controller, so plan for that. Example from the guide: db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity. Afterwards, verify with show db-protection-scheme, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and whose integrity-algorithm reports hmac-sha2-512 or none. db-migrate is the RPC through which the db-protection-scheme mode is changed.

Run show db-protection-scheme and read integrity-status. Its values are passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup and disabled, so passed-on-bootup is the confirmation you want; disabled means integrity checking is not in effect. The same command shows encryption-algorithm (xts-aes-256-plain64, AES-256 in XTS mode with 64-byte block size), integrity-algorithm (hmac-sha2-512 or none), and mode, the current protection scheme, which is either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is changed via the db-migrate RPC. Syntax: show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]. Available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. A node with integrity off displays integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled, mode encryption-only.

Use diff [-t|-c] candidate, which compares the candidate datastore against the current system configuration. It must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It reports created, deleted and changed objects and shows only configurable attributes; new data means the candidate configuration and old data means the current system configuration. Output forms: default normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values; -t for a side-by-side table diff; -c to render the differences as CLI commands that reproduce the same configuration; and -d to list the commands being executed. So yes, diff -c candidate gives you commands. There is also diff commit <id> [<id>], which compares a commit-record against the running configuration or against another commit-record cumulatively; it is available only when commit-tracking is enabled or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run discard-changes. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. It takes no parameters and no flags, and its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode, so you issue it from inside the candidate session you want to abandon. Nothing is committed and the running configuration is untouched. If instead you want to undo a change that has already been committed, use rollback commit [<commit-id>], and note that a rollback into the Candidate Datastore is only allowed when that candidate is empty.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration switch that introduces exceptional behaviour globally in the system, so treat it with care and only enable one you understand. The commands are add extended-config-<name>, delete extended-config-<name> and show extended-config-<name> [description]. The name is a string of 0..64 characters and must match a name already known by the system, so you need to know the valid extended-config name up front. Before adding one, read its description (string 0..255), which the system supplies and which states the effect that extended-config has on the system. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Check the service-impact attribute in the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]. service-impact is either service-affecting or non-service-affecting; if it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations, before applying the change. Alongside it, configuration-impact tells you the configuration steps needed to apply the change: no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change or full-config-no-pll-change. supported-values lists the permitted input ranges or discrete numbers, multiplicity (uint8) is how many values you must enter, and direction is transmit, receive or transmit-and-receive. All attributes are read-only. Example: show golden-advanced-parameter-chm7/EEPNNLMitigation.

Use lock, which locks database access to the current session and grants that session exclusive write access. It is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small period of time. While the database is locked, any other session, CLI or otherwise, that tries to make a configuration change receives an error. You cannot take the lock if another session is already holding it. The lock is released either by issuing unlock, or by the locking session closing, whether the user closes it explicitly, an administrator closes it, or it ends through inactivity time-out. Syntax is lock [-h], where -h displays help; there are no other parameters. Access mode is Operational Mode.

A named-value-set is addressed by a two-part key: named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that named-value-set. It holds a value item, a string of 1 to 1024 characters. The full command set is add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>], set with the same form to change the value, show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value] to read it, and delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> to remove it. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

It does if recovery from chassis storage is enabled. Check and set it with show recovery and set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value>. The values are disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration on this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then you issue a manual clear recovery-mode command, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the hardware), and auto-in-service (SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on a successful restore the NC automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service, so by default a replacement controller does pick the configuration up on its own. show recovery also reports restore-status (init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore), backup-status (successful, failed, in-progress, unknown), last-backup and next-backup.

Only if the candidate is empty. rollback commit [<commit-id>] works in the Running Datastore by default or in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if that candidate is empty, which is in fact a way to initialise the candidate.
