Use 'show current-subscription-<subscription-name> [related-session-id] [related-dial-out-server] [session-type] [session-protocol] [encoding] [transfer-mode] [updates-only] [user-access]'. encoding specifies the data encoding scheme for data sent to and from the target device and may be json, bytes, proto, ascii or json-ietf, defaulting to json-ietf. transfer-mode is stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off) or poll (values sent in response to a poll request), defaulting to stream. session-protocol is gnmi, default gnmi. session-type is gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel or gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc. updates-only is true/false, default false; when true the device sends only changes, not the initial current value. subscription-name is a string of length 0...128. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No, they are not all loaded by default: the 'enabled' attribute on data-model defaults to false. Use 'set data-model-<name> [enabled <value>]' with enabled true to load a model, and 'show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled]' to inspect it. 'show data-model' with no key lists all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. The 'enabled' attribute takes true or false and allows you to load/unload the data model; a loaded data model means it can be used via the management interfaces. 'name' is the model name, a string of length 0..256, used in set and show. 'description' is the data model description, string length 0..256, show only. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The dial-out-server retry-policy attribute takes progressive-back-off (the default), retry-then-stop, or retry-forever. The 'retry' attribute is the number of retries and applies only when retry-policy is retry-then-stop; it is an integer in the range 0..5 with default 3. 'timeout' is the timeout before the next retry, an integer 1..255 seconds with default 10, and it is not applicable for progressive-back-off, which has a dynamic timeout. The port is 'port', integer range 1..65535, default 4334, which is the default for the netconf protocol over ssh; 'protocol' is netconf (default) or restconf, and 'transport' shows ssh. 'auto-connect' defaults to true; if false the server can still be connected manually via the call-home RPC. Configure with 'add/set dial-out-server-<name>'.

Yes, gNMI/gRPC is enabled by default: the grpc 'enabled' attribute is true/false with default true. The listening port is the 'port' attribute, which defaults to 50051 and is the port that listens for gNMI access via gRPC where gRPC is enabled. Use 'set grpc [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity <value>]' and 'show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]'. gnmi-get-encoding-granularity controls the granularity of data in gNMI Get responses when encoded with JSON: per-path puts all path data in one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; the default is per-object. The grpc object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

NETCONF listens on the 'port' attribute, a port-number (uint16, range 1..65535) with default 830, which is the port that listens for NETCONF access via ssh. The 'hello-timeout' attribute specifies the number of seconds a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; a session is dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that number of seconds elapses. It is a uint16 in the range 1..3600 seconds with a default of 2. Configure with 'set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [annotate-cli-name <value>] [static-info-in-notifs <value>] [hello-timeout <value>]' and inspect with 'show netconf'. 'enabled' defaults to true, and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session.

Plain HTTP exists but is off by default: 'http-enabled' is true/false with default false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. 'https-enabled' defaults to true. The ports are 'http-port', number range 1..65535 default 8080, and 'https-port', number range 1..65535 default 8181. Session lifetime is governed by 'cookie-timeout', the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, a number in the range 1..300 minutes with default 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. The overall 'enabled' switch defaults to true. Use 'set restconf [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [cookie-timeout]'; 'show restconf' also returns the read-only 'api-root' (string 0..64).

Use 'show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count]'. The snmp-engine-id attribute is the SNMP EngineID of the NE, a show-only string of length 0..256; the EngineID follows EngineID format 3 as defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the MAC address pool of the NE. The companion show-only attribute engine-boot-count is the SNMP engine boot count, a uint16 defaulting to 0, which counts how many times the engine has restarted. The settable attributes are 'enabled' (true/false, default true, global SNMP access) and 'port' (number 1..65535, default 161, where the NE listens for SNMP requests), via 'set snmp [enabled <value>] [port <value>]'. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. The snmp-community attribute community-string-access is the SNMP access right of the community string and its only permitted value is read-only, which is also the default. Create a community with 'add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>]', and modify it with 'set snmp-community-<name>'. 'name' is the name for the community, distinct from the community string itself, a string of length 0..64; 'community-string' is the community string itself, string length 1..32; 'enabled' is false/true with default true and switches the community string on or off. Delete with 'delete snmp-community-<name>'. Note the trap-community-string is not here, it is located in the snmp-target object.

Add a trap listener with 'add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]'. snmp-version takes v2c or v3 and defaults to v2c. trap-community-string is the community string used for SNMP traps, a string of length 0...32, defaulting to infinera. target-port is the UDP port number, range 0..65535, default 162, and target-transport is udp (default udp). target-name is a string 0...32; target-address is the IPv4/IPv6 address or hostname of the target; enabled defaults to true. snmpv3-user is applicable when snmp-version is v3. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

A new SNMPv3 user gets user-sec-level no-auth-no-priv, which is the default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy protocol attribute priv-protocol offers DES, AES128, AES192 and AES256, with AES128 as the default. The authentication protocol auth-protocol has SHA as its only value and default. Create with 'add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]', so both passphrases are required on add; each is a string of length 8...64. The user name is a string of length 1...32. Example: 'add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123'.

The subscription-path-mode attribute controls how subscription updates are sent: target-defined (the default), on-change, or sample. Inspect it with 'show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> [subscription-path] [subscription-path-origin] [subscription-path-mode] [sample-interval] [heartbeat-interval] [suppress-redundant]'. sample-interval is the time in milliseconds between samples of the telemetry data source, default 0 (set to 0 when optional); for a target-defined stream subscription, if sample-interval is not set the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. heartbeat-interval, default 0 ms, is the maximum interval that may pass between updates; if sample-interval is unset and heartbeat-interval is below 10 seconds the system adjusts it to 20 seconds. suppress-redundant is true/false, default true.

Use 'show subscriptions'. It shows a list of subscriptions, takes no parameters, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the detail behind each entry, use 'show current-subscription-<subscription-name>', which shows a list representation of the telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, with attributes such as related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. For the paths within a subscription, use 'show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>' or plain 'show subscription-path', which exposes subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode, sample-interval, heartbeat-interval and suppress-redundant.

Telemetry is configured through the telemetry command: 'show telemetry' and 'set telemetry id <string>'. The guide states this command is used to configure persistent and dynamic telemetry, and that the telemetry object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Its single parameter is 'id', described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, a string of length 0..4096 with no default. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The guide does not define the distinction between persistent and dynamic telemetry beyond that statement. Related views are 'show subscriptions', 'show current-subscription-<subscription-name>' (which distinguishes dial-in from dial-out session types) and 'show subscription-path'.

Use 'show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]', or 'show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]'. The 'state' attribute is the third party app state and takes running, stopped or failed, with a default of stopped. It is not enabled by default: the 'enable' attribute is the third-party-app enabled state, true or false, with default false; if enabled the app is started and is also enabled upon system restart, and if disabled the app is stopped. Set these with 'set third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]'. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Installed apps are removed with 'clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>'.

Type 'add <tab>' to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time, and 'add -h' for help; the add command page also lists the creatable entities in the add Command Entities table (aaa-server, access-rule, ace, acl, adg, card, chassis, dial-out-server, interface, ipv4-address, log-file, ntp-server, odu, otu, snmp-community, snmp-target, snmpv3-user, tom, user, user-group, xcon and others), each with a page cross-reference to its own command section where the parameters are listed. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided on creation; if a mandatory attribute is not given in the command itself, the CLI automatically asks for it. Use 'add -v <entity id>' to validate a command without creating anything. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with add.

Yes. In all cases the clear command requires a user confirmation, and a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided. Use 'clear -f ...' to force the command without confirmation. The syntax is 'clear [-f] <subcommand> ...', with subcommands alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, dns, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, statistics, system and topology. 'clear -h' displays help. Access mode is Operational Mode. Note that 'clear system factory-reset' with the shutdown option is not supported on the L0 cards. Confirmation can also be suppressed per session by setting interactive-mode false on cli-session-config, which makes the CLI suppress any prompt to the user.

Yes, with the cli attribute show-alarm-columns, which sets the columns displayed in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma, 'default-columns' to show the pre-defined columns, or 'default-columns,<additional-details>' to add the <additional-details> column to the pre-defined columns. The default is default-columns. This configuration has a global effect and takes effect on all CLI sessions. Set it with 'set cli show-alarm-columns <value>', for example 'set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3' or 'set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action' to show the corrective-action column as the last column. Read it back with 'show cli show-alarm-columns'. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use 'set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>'. cli-lines is the configurable number of rows used for display before pausing the output, a number in the range 10..1000 with default 40; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes the display. The companion attribute cli-columns is the configurable number of columns used for display, range 80..4000 with default 80. Read them back with 'show cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines] [cli-columns] [interactive-mode] [display-timestamp]'. session-id is a string, for example 10.19.204.27:52361, so 'set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30' sets 30 rows. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Yes. The connect command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI: 'connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>]'. target-address may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or a hostname if DNS is configured; it requires connectivity and is a mandatory attribute. user-name is a string of 0..64 characters. port is optional; by default port 22 is used, but a port can be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Access mode is Operational Mode. Example: 'connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022', which adds the host to the known hosts list and then prompts for the password of admin@10.41.24.55.

Yes, use the convert command: 'convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>'. target-representation may be netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (the same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted, snmp-oids (the OIDs for objects in a show command) or netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing an SNMP request). The command string should be enclosed in quotes; multiple CLI commands separated by ';' are merged into one payload where possible. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto filled, only the password must be entered.

No. The default command assigns default values to the targeted entities and is useful to reset an entity after changes, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes that are only settable at creation. Syntax is 'default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*]'. If attributes are specified only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation and -h displays help. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard '*', for example 'default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*' or 'default alarm-severity-entry-*'; 'default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode' defaults just those two. Not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: 'delete -b <object>'. Introduced in R9.0, best effort delete bypasses the check for object existence without returning a failure, so unlike the standard 'delete <object>' which fails if the object does not exist, 'delete -b <object>' does not fail when the object is missing. It has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. Note that -b only suppresses the missing-object error; it may still produce other errors, such as precondition failures. Full syntax is 'delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]'. For scripting you will usually also want -f, which forces the command without confirmation, since delete otherwise displays a confirmation prompt; -v validates only and replies 'OK' without deleting.

The exit command logs you out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operational mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided, so 'exit -f' exits without confirmation. The syntax is 'exit [-h|-f]', where -h displays help for the command and -f forces the command without confirmation. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as 'exit -f'. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use the expect command: 'expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>'. It validates an existing attribute value against an expected value; if the value matches, no output is seen, but if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and automation to guarantee specific assumptions and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes. Wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. If the script runs in 'stop-on-error' mode, a failed expect stops the script immediately. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string. Examples: 'expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123' and 'expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*'.

Yes, use the export command: 'export [<variable>=[<value>]]', available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Variables are referenced as ${variable} in any CLI command, which makes them useful in CLI scripts. The variable name can be any alphanumeric name; the value is a string that can contain any supported character, including spaces. They do not survive logout: variables are defined locally per session and are removed after the session is closed. 'export SLOT_NUMBER=2' declares a variable, 'export SLOT_NUMBER=' deletes it, and 'export' with no arguments lists all existing variables, for example MYSESSIONID and MYUSERNAME.

Both launch a Linux bash shell from the CLI in Operational Mode, and both accept a single command to execute instead of an interactive session; 'exit' returns you to the CLI prompt. 'shell [-h] [shell command]' opens a shell on the node itself, running as the currently logged in user with that user's command access; certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted binaries include /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and the /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin/*.sh scripts). 'gshell [-h] [<cmd>]' instead opens the bash shell inside the Guest Container, for example 'gshell ls -l'; its pre-condition is that the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly.

No. 'kill-session <session-id>' closes any established session regardless of type (CLI, NETCONF, etc), and the <session-id> must match an existing session-id in the form '<ip-address>:<port>', but it cannot match the id of your current session. To end your own session use the normal 'exit' command instead. Use 'show session' first to display the list of current sessions and get the correct session-id. Access Mode is Operational mode. Example: 'kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212'.

Use the message command: 'message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]', Operational mode. The message content is a string of 1 to 4096 characters. The target defaults to 'all', so 'message "System will reboot in 5 minutes"' broadcasts to every CLI session. Other target values are: local (only serial console or CRAFT sessions), remote (only remote sessions such as SSH), a session-id for one specific session, or a username to reach all CLI sessions of that user. Example targeted form: 'message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36'. The command can also be issued over NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only delivered to CLI sessions.

Card properties are type-specific, auto instantiated by the system but user configurable, addressed as property-<card-name>/<property-name>. Syntax: 'set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]' and 'show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]', in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Two properties are supported: fast-client-recovery, which indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures, with values disabled or enabled and default disabled; and max-packet-length, the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO, with a range of 1518 to 18000 and default 1518. Example: 'set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled'.

Use the run command, in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. Pre-condition: the task or the script to be called must already be defined. For a task: 'run task [[task-name=]<value>]', where task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name, for example 'run task collect-diag'. For a script: 'run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]', where script-name is a relative path to the script directory and arguments are optional. Flags: -q runs in quiet mode showing only command output rather than commands plus output; -r executes the script as a declarative config script, replacing system configuration with the script content; -e sets the error option, continue (default), stop, or rollback. Example: 'run script config.cli -e=stop -q'.

Both define user-configurable scheduled commands via add/set/show/delete in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and share enabled (true/false, default true), command, command-type (CLI), frequency in w/d/h/m/s, start-time, end-time and persistent (true/false, default true, persists a system restart). 'task' is the fuller object: 'add task-<name> command <value> ...' adds label, alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and number-of-runs (no-limit, or 1..65535) for periodic tasks, name is a string 0..64, command 1..1024, and its read-only task-status values are scheduled, disabled, finished, ongoing with previous-result success or fail. 'scheduled-task' uses 'add/set scheduled-task-<name>', is listed with 'show scheduled-tasks', takes command length 0..1024, timestamps in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, task-status true/false default false, and previous-result 1 or 2.

Only if you are an SA user. 'show session' lists the currently established management layer sessions, but only SA users can access the list of all sessions; all remaining users can only see their own session. Syntax: 'show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]', Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. session-id is the IP address and transport port of the session, or 'NA' if the session was initiated from the serial port. session-type may be cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui or gnmi, and session-protocol may be telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https or http. RESTCONF sessions appear only with Cookie Based Authentication; the keep-alive defaults to 5 minutes and is changed with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute.

Yes. 'set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]' can set an attribute on multiple instances at once using the wildcard '*': as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), of a single instance key (port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*, ethernet-*) and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* instead of admin-state). Ranges and lists are written with brackets: card-1-[1..4], interface-[DCN,CRAFT]. You can also narrow the scope with filters of the form <attribute>=<value>, as in 'set port port-type=line admin-state lock'. All pairs must belong to the same managed entity. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates.

User access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE, and TT user-groups. The command 'shell [-h] [shell command]' runs in Operational Mode and launches a Linux bash shell as the currently logged in user, allowing the commands accessible to that user; exit the shell the usual way (for example 'exit') to return to the CLI prompt. A single command can also be run inline, as in 'shell ifconfig' or 'shell vi'. Certain commands and scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo', including /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient, and the scripts under /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin/ such as download.sh, install_os.sh and docker.sh.

Yes. If a user executes a show command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Reduce the scope rather than widening it: address a specific <entity-id> instead of a generic <entity-type>, limit recursion with '-r=<n>' (n levels down, full recursion if n is omitted), restrict what is returned with '-c' (container instances only), '-a' (attributes only), '-x' (configuration/read-write attributes only) or '-o' (state/read-only attributes only), or apply filters of the form <attribute>=<value>. For long but legal output, page it with '<command> | more', which must be the last piped command in the line.

Yes, with the simulate command in Operational mode: 'simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>])'. The trigger values are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru, though plug-out-fru is not supported. For equipment simulation you supply the holder-AID (string 1..64, matching the card slot or tom port) and, for a plug-in, the card type, with subtype optional. For alarms you supply alarmed-entity and alarm-type; if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared. alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto, selected by the system. It works on a simulator and on a real system, but a simulation that interferes with real hardware is rejected, for example you cannot simulate plugout of hardware that is physically present.

Yes. 'sleep <time in seconds>' specifies a delay for the given amount of time, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. 'sleep 1' waits one second and 'sleep 0.1' waits 100 milliseconds. The command runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, and 'sleep -h' displays its help.

Use the task command and give a start-time but no frequency, since frequency is only set for periodic tasks. Syntax: 'add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]'. The guide's example is exactly a one-off database backup: 'add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once"'. This requires that the file server xfr1 be configured before the command is used. name is a string 0..64, command 1..1024, command-type defaults to cli, enabled defaults to true, persistent defaults to true so the task survives a system restart, and alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited (default allowed). After it runs, 'show task-<name>' reports task-status finished and previous-result success or fail.

'terminate' stops a running operation in Operational Mode, in these forms: 'terminate location-led <entity>' for a location led test previously started by activate, where the entity can be a chassis or a card; 'terminate otdr [entity=]<value>' to stop an ongoing OTDR measurement on a port; 'terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>' to stop a manually triggered OTDR based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity; 'terminate loopback [entity=]<value> [, <value>]*' to terminate WSS loopback on NMC entities, where all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated; and 'terminate cable-id' for a CableID verification test. Invoking location-led termination when no test is active has no effect. For CableID, the current port-pair test always runs to completion first, so the maximum delay is one port-pair verification time, and you confirm the stop with 'show cable-id cable-id-status' once cable-id-state reads idle.

'update' does not assign an arbitrary attribute value the way set does; it triggers a specific predefined update action on an object, selected by <type>. Syntax: 'update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*]', Operational mode, and multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard '*'. The supported type values are: span-loss-alarm-threshold, which updates (re-evaluates) the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold; filter-insertion-date-now, which updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date; set-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to under commissioning state, applicable to NE entities in SLTE systems; and clear-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to Ready for Service state, also for SLTE NE entities. Examples: 'update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line' and 'update filter-insertion-date-now chassis'.

Use the auxiliary commands tic and toc. 'tic' starts a timer for the typed command and 'toc' displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Put them either side of the command on one line, separated by semicolons: 'tic;show log;toc'. The same pattern works around a list of commands in a script, for example 'tic ;show log ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 ;toc'. These are add-on commands intended for exactly this kind of use, evaluating the system response to a command or script.

Yes, use 'help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...]'. It searches the provided keywords in all commands help text and displays the matches in order of relevance. Multiple keywords can be given and the result includes commands matching either keyword, for example 'help -s database 'cold restart''. Partial keywords are supported with a wildcard, as in 'help -s data*' or 'help -s *config*', which matches ifconfig, config and configuration. Results appear as a list of help commands you can then run to view the entire help text, each with an excerpt of the help text and the target keyword underlined. The search only provides matches in the scope of commands and system features; object and attribute matches are excluded. Related help forms are 'help <command>', '?', '<command> ?', '<command> -?' and '<command> -h'.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions. The alias command defines a friendlier alphanumeric string for one or more commands, containers, attributes or values, in Operational mode. Syntax: 'alias [-h]' and 'alias [<name>=<value>]'. With no arguments it prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Multi word values must be quoted, for example 'alias sa='show alarm'', while a single word alias is simply 'alias s=show'. Aliases can reference other aliases, and the <name> of an alias can be used without resolving it by putting it in quotes. Remove aliases with the unalias command, which likewise has impact on all sessions and users.

Run 'unalias -a', which removes all alias definitions. The unalias command removes previously defined aliases in Operational Mode; syntax is 'unalias -h', 'unalias -a' and 'unalias [<name> ...]', so you can also drop specific ones, as in 'unalias foo' or 'unalias bar baz qux'. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Removing an alias will have impact on all sessions and users, since aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so 'unalias -a' clears them for everyone, not just your session. Use 'alias' with no arguments beforehand to review the current list.

Use the tree flags: 'tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...])'. '-d=depth' sets the maximum display depth, the number of levels to be displayed; if not specified all levels are displayed by default, so 'tree -d=2' caps the listing at two levels from the current scope. '-a' displays entity ancestors only, that is the target entity along with all its ancestors, for example 'tree -a interface-DCN' or 'tree -a port usb'. '-o' displays the YANG tree of the provided top node. The base of the tree is the current working entity or the provided entity id, only managed entities are shown with no attribute names or values, and output uses the UTF-8 character set. You can also page it with 'tree | more'. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

All three change the currently selected managed entity, and the effect is visible in the CLI path banner. 'edit <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...]' navigates to any entity in the hierarchy; the IDs can be absolute from the root of the system or relative to the current entity, and editing a nonexistent entity instance fails. For example 'edit card-1-1' is absolute and 'edit chassis-1 slot-2' reaches the same place relatively. 'up' brings the current path up by exactly one level, to the parent of the current entity, and takes no parameters other than -h. 'top' jumps straight to the top of the managed entity hierarchy, the [ne] level. All three run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode and accept '-h' for help.

Use the history command, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. 'history' displays the current session's command history as a numbered list. Each command can be repeated using '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list, and '!!' repeats the previous command. To find a particular entry in a long list, filter with piped commands, for example 'history | include 'show''. The only flag is '-h', which displays help for the command.

Nothing happens: at the hierarchy top level the 'up' command has no impact. 'up' brings the current path up by one path level, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent, and its effect is visible on the CLI banner; once the banner already reads [ne] there is no parent to move to. The command supports no parameters other than '-h', and runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands are 'edit', which navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, and 'top', which goes directly to the top of the hierarchy root.

They filter identically: both 'include' and 'grep' are piped commands that display only the lines matching <filter>, and the guide states each is the same as the other. For both, the filter may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed in quotes, supports regex, does a case insensitive comparison (so 'show | grep abc' equals 'show | grep ABC'), and multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. The difference is that grep has several additional filtering options: '<command> | grep [<option>] <filter>' accepts '-a=<n>' for the number of lines of context to show after the actual match, '-b=<n>' for the number of lines of context before the match, and '-n' to display line numbers in the result. 'include' has only '-h' and <filter>. The counterpart filter is 'exclude'.

Yes. Pipe the output through the `display` piped command using the `commands` mode: `<command> | display <mode>`. The `commands` mode displays the configurations as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, and the guide states it is useful for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. The documented example for producing a CLI script from all system configurations is `show -r | display commands`. The other supported modes for the show command are list (the default display mode, one value per line), table, csv, keys-table, single-table, only-values (only the value of the requested attributes, useful for script building), xml, json, xpath, and interactive. `display -h` shows help for the command.

Yes. Combine the `begin` and `until` piped commands; the guide states explicitly that `begin` can be used together with the 'until' piped command to retrieve a sub-set of an output. `begin <words>` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, and the output begins with the line that matches the word. `until <words>` displays the output ending at a specified word, and the output ends with the line that matches the word. For both, <words> is the line to begin with / end with, and it may contain spaces if in quotes. Each also accepts -h for help. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` and `show | until ne-location`.

Yes, and the position matters. The `more` piped command displays long outputs incrementally, page by page: `<command> | more [-h]`. Multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, i.e. it is related to the terminal size, except for the serial port case where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display is paused; press any key to resume, or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space> and <tab>) shows the next page. Example: `tree | include led | more`.

It does not fail. The `sort` piped command reorders the output of a show command, and if an unrecognized attribute name is used it is ignored. Syntax: `<show command> | sort [-h]` or `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`, where <attribute> is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output. Yes, you can flip the order: -i inverts the order in the output, and it can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. Sort without parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display. Examples: `show card | sort`, `show port | sort port-type`, `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date`, and `show odu | sort -i`.

Capitalisation does not matter, and yes, patterns are supported. The `exclude` piped command filters out lines that contain a defined word or string: `<command> | exclude <filter>` (or `exclude -h` for help). <filter> does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and it may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed by quotes. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. Examples: `show | exclude ne`, `show | exclude 'ne oper'`, and `show led | exclude status`. Related commands are `include`, which filters output that includes the filtering text, and `grep`, which is the same as `include`.

Yes. The `highlight` piped command visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of the previous command: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`, with `highlight -h` for help. More than one word can be provided. Words given without quotes are searched for separately; to mark up a whole phrase, enclose it in quotes so it is searched for as a sentence. <word> is any word to highlight and may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. Examples: `show odu | highlight odu4` highlights one word; `show odu | hightlight odu4 oduflex` highlights the two words separately; and `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4` highlights the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' plus the word 'odu4'.

Yes. The `linenum` piped command adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax: `<command> | linenum`, or `<command> | linenum -h` to display help. It takes no other parameters; <command> is any display command such as tree or show. Example: `show | linenum` displays an output with enumerated lines. As an alternative when you are already filtering, the `grep` piped command supports the -n option, which displays line numbers in the result, alongside -a=<n> (number of lines of context to show after the actual match) and -b=<n> (number of lines of context to show before the actual match).
